p: Welcome to the first lesson on how wine is made, and we start where every wine starts: in the vineyard. In this lesson we look at the vine as a living plant, at what it needs to grow, at the four parts of a grape, and at the journey from a tiny flower to a bunch of ripe fruit. By the end you will understand why a grape's colour, sugar, acidity, tannin and flavours change over the summer, and why that matters so much in the glass.

First, the vine itself. A vine can live for sixty years or more, and every year it repeats the same cycle. In spring it wakes up and grows new shoots, leaves and flowers. Over the summer the flowers turn into grapes, and by the end of summer those grapes are ripe. In autumn the vine drops its leaves, and in winter it rests, dormant, without growing at all. Wine grapes are not picked from wild plants: they come from carefully managed vineyards, where growers keep the vines under control to get a healthy crop every year.

There are several species of vine, some native to Europe and Asia, others to North America. But almost every wine in the world is made from just one European species. Within that species there are many varieties, just as there are many kinds of apple. Each variety has its own look and its own taste. Riesling and Cabernet Sauvignon, for example, differ not only in colour but also in flavour. Much of this course is about getting to know these varieties one by one.

Now, what does a vine need? Five things: warmth, sunlight, carbon dioxide, water and nutrients. Because a vine is rooted in one spot, it must take all of them either from the soil, through its roots, or from the air, through its leaves. The sun supplies heat and light. Without enough heat the vine simply cannot grow, which is exactly why it goes dormant in winter. The roots also take up small amounts of nutrients, needed to build healthy shoots, leaves and roots.

Sunlight has a very special job. It powers photosynthesis: the vine combines carbon dioxide, drawn in by the leaves, with water, drawn up by the roots, and turns them into sugar. That sugar is the vine's fuel. It feeds the growth of the plant and ripens the grapes. So when you taste a ripe, sweet grape, you are really tasting stored sunshine, and this is the sugar that yeast will later turn into alcohol.

Let's open a grape and look inside. There are four parts to know. The skin, together with the layer just beneath it, is where most of the flavour is found. The skin also holds colour and tannin, and black grapes have far more of both than white grapes. The pulp is mostly water and sugar, with acids and flavours too. Then there are the seeds and the stems, which are rich in tannin and can make a wine taste very bitter if they are handled roughly in the winery.

Here is a detail that surprises many people. With only a handful of exceptions, the pulp of black grapes is just as pale as the pulp of white grapes. So the colour of a red wine does not come from the juice: it comes from the skins. That is why a white wine can be made from black grapes, as long as the juice is kept away from the skins, while a red wine needs time in contact with them to gain its colour and its tannin.

Now the grape's year. In spring the vine produces small clusters of flowers, and each cluster will become a bunch of grapes. Every single flower must be pollinated to become a grape. Many plants rely on bright petals to attract insects, but the vine does not need them: it pollinates itself. This stage is called flowering. Once a flower has been pollinated, it starts to grow seeds and to swell. At that moment it has become a grape, and we call this fruit set.

Newly formed grapes are small, hard, green and unpleasant to eat. Over the summer they grow, and by mid-summer they are big enough for the vine to start ripening them. Ripening begins with véraison, the moment the grapes lose their green colour. White grapes turn golden, while black grapes turn red and then purple. If you ever walk through a vineyard in mid-summer, look for bunches with a mix of green and coloured berries: that is véraison happening before your eyes.

What changes during ripening? At the start, a grape is unripe: very high in acid, with hardly any sugar and an unattractive, green, herbaceous taste. As it ripens it swells with water and becomes soft and fleshy. The acidity falls and the sugar rises. The herbaceous notes fade and the variety's signature flavours appear. In some white grapes, aromas move from green fruit, like apple, to stone fruit, like peach, and then to tropical fruit. In black grapes, they move from fresh fruit towards cooked fruit.

Black grapes go through one more important change: the tannins in their skins ripen. Tannin gives red wine its grip, the drying feeling on your gums. Ripe tannins feel smooth; unripe tannins taste bitter and harsh. So a grower picking black grapes must check not only the sugar but also the tannins. A grape can be sweet enough and still have unripe tannins, and the wine would show it.

And if the grapes stay on the vine even longer? They become extra-ripe. This only works if the weather stays dry, because rain brings fungal disease, and warm enough for ripening to continue. At first the aromas become exaggeratedly ripe and the sugar keeps climbing. Later, water evaporates, the grapes shrivel like raisins, and their sugars and acids become concentrated, with dried-fruit aromas. Such grapes can be so sweet at harvest that they are usually made into sweet wines. We will come back to this in the lesson on vineyard choices.

A memory tip: think of a grape as a traffic light. Green and hard means stop: lots of acid, little sugar, herbaceous flavours. Golden or purple means go: sugar up, acid down, real fruit flavours and, in black grapes, ripe tannins. Leave it longer and the light turns to a deep amber: shrivelled, concentrated, perfect for sweet wines.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, a vine needs warmth, sunlight, carbon dioxide, water and nutrients, and sunlight lets it turn carbon dioxide and water into sugar. Second, the skin gives flavour, colour and tannin, the pulp gives water, sugar and acid, seeds and stems give bitter tannin, and red colour comes from black skins, not the juice. Third, the grape's year runs from flowering to fruit set to véraison, and as it ripens acid falls, sugar rises, flavours ripen and, in black grapes, tannins ripen too.

In this lesson we ask a simple question: how much heat and light reach the grapes? Almost everything here comes back to that. We will look at cool, moderate and warm climates, then at the natural features that make a place warmer or cooler, such as latitude, altitude, seas, rivers, fog and soil. After that we turn to weather, the surprises of each year, and finally we link it all to ripeness, wine style and quality.

First, let's separate two words that are often mixed up. Climate is the average pattern of temperature, sunlight and rainfall that a region can expect year after year: weather over the long term. Weather is what actually happens, day by day. Climate does not change from one year to the next, but it can shift over decades. Today records show air and ocean temperatures rising, with more extreme events such as droughts and floods, and more and more producers are working to adapt and to limit the effects.

One of the most useful ways to classify a climate is by the heat available during the growing season. In the northern hemisphere that season runs from April to October; in the southern hemisphere, from October to April. We use three bands, based on the average temperature over the season. Cool means sixteen and a half degrees Celsius or below. Moderate means between sixteen and a half and eighteen and a half. Warm means between eighteen and a half and twenty-one degrees.

Why does temperature matter so much? Because it decides which grapes can succeed in a region and which flavours they develop. Some varieties, like Grenache, only ripen properly in warm climates. Others, like Chardonnay, grow happily almost anywhere but change character with the heat: lean and citrusy in a cool place, round and tropical in a warm one. So the same grape can give very different wines depending on where it is planted.

Now the factors that shape a region's climate. The most important is latitude, the distance from the equator. The closer to the equator, the hotter it is likely to be. Most vineyards lie between thirty and fifty degrees north or south. Outside that band it is usually too hot or too cold for vines to survive. Then comes altitude: temperature drops as you climb, so a vineyard high on a hillside is always cooler than one at the same latitude down on the plain.

Mountains can also act as a shield. They shelter vineyards from cloud, rain and cold winds, which brings sunny summers, dry autumns and a long growing season. Slope and aspect matter too. Far from the equator, heat and light are scarce. But a vineyard on a slope facing the equator catches the sun more directly, so it gives riper grapes than flat land or a slope facing away. In the northern hemisphere that means south-facing slopes; in the southern hemisphere, north-facing ones.

Water nearby changes the picture as well. Seas have a moderating effect. In warm regions near the coast, cold ocean currents cool things down, as in the vineyards of South Africa's Cape. In northern Europe, by contrast, warm currents bring welcome warmth. Moving air helps too: cool breezes blow in from cold seas onto warm coasts, and at night cold air slides down from mountains into lower vineyards, cooling the heat built up during the day.

Rivers warm up and cool down more slowly than land. In autumn they are warmer than the ground around them, so in cool regions they keep vineyards a little warmer, help protect them against frost and stretch out the ripening season. They can also reflect sunlight onto the vines, a real help far from the equator. And the morning mists that rise from rivers in autumn are essential for noble rot, the friendly fungus behind some famous sweet wines.

Cloud, fog and mist are all water vapour we can see. Clouds form above the ground and can block sunlight, slowing photosynthesis so the grapes ripen more slowly: an important cooling factor in some warmer Australian regions. Fog forms at ground level and chills the vineyard; it is a key influence in coastal parts of California and Chile. Mist is simply a thinner fog. Finally, soil. It must hold enough water and nutrients to keep the vine healthy, and stones on the surface soak up heat and warm the vineyard, helping ripening.

Now weather, the year's surprises. In a cool vintage, with lower temperatures and weaker sunlight than usual, the grapes struggle to ripen: acid stays too high, sugar too low, and the signature aromas may not develop. In a hot vintage, grapes can show odd dried-fruit aromas and even get sunburnt. Heat also makes the vine thirsty, and hot weather usually means little rain. Short of water, the vine shuts down to protect itself and the grapes stop ripening.

Drought, a long spell of below-average rain, often made worse by heat, can stop ripening and, at worst, kill the vine. Irrigation helps, but in a drought there may be no water to use. Heavy rain is a problem too: damp spreads fungal disease, and a downpour just before harvest makes the grapes swell with water and dilutes their flavours. Hail can shred vines and destroy a whole year's crop in minutes. And spring frost can kill the young shoots, which means fewer grapes that year.

So how does all this connect to style and quality? Follow the chain: cause, ripeness, style. Less heat and light means grapes with more acid, less sugar and less-ripe flavours, giving fresher, crisper wines. More heat and light means less acid, more sugar and riper flavours, giving rounder, fuller wines. Quality depends on balance: too little warmth leaves grapes sour and thin, too much brings cooked flavours and stress. And because weather changes each year, the same vineyard can give very different vintages.

A memory tip: picture every factor as a dial on a heater. Being closer to the equator, sun-facing slopes, stones, mountain shelter and rivers in autumn turn the heat up. Altitude, cold currents, sea breezes, fog and cloud turn it down. Whenever an exam question names a feature, ask yourself: does this turn the heater up or down? Then you know whether the grapes will be riper or fresher.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, climate is the long-term average and weather is what happens each year; cool is up to sixteen and a half degrees in the growing season, moderate up to eighteen and a half, warm up to twenty-one. Second, latitude is the main climate factor, with vineyards between thirty and fifty degrees, while altitude, slope, seas, rivers, fog and soil fine-tune it. Third, frost, hail, drought, heavy rain and extreme vintages change both the quantity and the quality of each year's crop.

In this lesson we put on our boots and follow the grower through the year. Nature sets the stage, but people make many decisions that shape the grapes. We will look at training and pruning, at irrigation, at the fight against weeds, pests and diseases, and at what organic growing means. Then we turn to yield and the timing of the harvest, and we finish with the three ways of concentrating sugar in grapes for sweet wines: extra-ripeness, noble rot and frozen grapes.

First, the goal. A grower wants a healthy, regular crop every single year, big enough to be commercially worthwhile. Left alone, a vine would sprawl like a bramble, with tangled shoots and an irregular crop. So growers do two things. They train the vine, giving it a shape, and most vines around the world are trained on trellises, rows of posts and wires that hold up the shoots and bunches. And they prune it, usually in winter while the vine is dormant, cutting back the old growth so that each vine keeps its required shape.

Next, water. In regions where rain is scarce, growers are usually allowed to irrigate. There are many ways to do it, from simply flooding the field to drip systems with a small pipe that waters each vine individually. But water is an increasingly limited and expensive resource, so most growers now use it sparingly. And remember what we saw in the last lesson: in a real drought, irrigation may be impossible because there is simply no water left.

Now the enemies. Vines are vulnerable to many fungal diseases. Fungi grow on the grapes and on the leaves and can cut both the quality and the quantity of the crop, sometimes dramatically. Damp weather and rain help them spread. Then come pests: small insects, but also larger animals and birds that love ripe grapes. Animals and birds can be kept out with fences and nets. Nets also have another use: in some regions, such as parts of Argentina, they protect vines from hail.

Fungi and insects are much harder to control. One option is chemical sprays. Fungicides kill fungi, insecticides kill insects, and herbicides keep weeds under control in vineyards where they are a problem. The trouble is that some of these chemicals can cause longer-term problems in the vineyard, so many growers try to use as few as possible. If a vineyard is certified organic, its grapes are grown without most chemicals. Note the word most: some sprays are still allowed, to keep the worst fungal diseases in check. When you see the word organic on a label, this is what it tells you.

Now yield. Yield is the amount of fruit a vineyard produces per unit of area, for example per hectare. A vine with enough heat, sunlight, water, nutrients and carbon dioxide can give a commercial crop of ripe grapes. But the size of that crop matters. If yields are too high, the vine spreads its energy over too many grapes, which can end up with diluted flavours and less sugar. If yields are too low, the crop is too small to pay the bills. In some regions, the law sets a maximum yield.

Then comes one of the grower's biggest decisions: when to pick. Grapes harvested early have less sugar, more acidity and less-ripe flavours, a good starting point for fresh, crisp wines. Grapes harvested later have more sugar, less acidity and riper flavours. Leave them on the vine for a very long time and they begin to shrivel, concentrating their sugar even further and taking on raisin and dried-fruit flavours.

How are grapes picked? By hand or by machine. Here is a point that often appears in exams: neither method is fundamentally better for quality. The choice usually depends on the style of wine being made. There is one practical limit, though. Machine harvesters cannot work on steep slopes, so on very steep vineyards picking by hand is the only option.

Finally, sweet wines. To make them, you need grapes that are extremely rich in sugar, and there are three main ways to get there. The first is extra-ripeness. The grapes stay on the vine well past the normal harvest. This only works if the weather stays dry, because rain brings rot, and warm enough for ripening to continue. First the sugar rises and the aromas become very ripe. Then the water evaporates, the grapes shrivel and their sugars and acids become concentrated, with dried-fruit aromas.

The second way is noble rot. It is caused by a fungus called botrytis. The fungus pierces tiny holes in the grape skin, water evaporates through them, and the sugars, acids and flavours become concentrated. But botrytis is a double-edged sword: in the wrong conditions it simply destroys the crop. To be noble, it must attack grapes that are already ripe, and it needs a special rhythm of weather: damp, misty mornings that help it grow and spread, followed by warm, dry afternoons that hold it back. Those autumn mists often rise from nearby rivers. Grapes with noble rot are nearly always made into sweet wines.

The third way is freezing. In some regions, healthy grapes are left on the vine through autumn and into winter. When the temperature drops low enough, the water inside them turns to ice. The grapes are picked while frozen and pressed before they thaw. The ice crystals stay behind with the skins, and only a small amount of liquid flows out, very rich in sugar, acid and flavour. The result is icewine: sweet, concentrated, and with a remarkably pure taste of the grape variety.

A memory tip for the three sweet routes: the sun, the fog and the frost. The sun keeps working on grapes left late on the vine until they shrivel. The fog of misty mornings lets noble rot do its work. And the frost turns the water in the grapes to ice, leaving a tiny drop of concentrated juice. Three different routes, one goal: less water, more sugar.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, vines are trained, mostly on trellises, and pruned in winter, irrigation is used where rain is scarce, and organic growing avoids most chemicals but still allows some sprays against the worst fungal diseases. Second, yields that are too high dilute flavour and sugar, early picking gives more acid and fresher flavours, late picking gives more sugar and riper flavours, and hand and machine harvesting are equally good for quality, though machines cannot work steep slopes. Third, sugar for sweet wines can be concentrated by extra-ripeness, by noble rot, or by freezing the grapes on the vine.

In this lesson we learn to read a wine label like a map. Many labels tell you first of all where the grapes were grown, and in Europe that place name also hides a set of rules. We will see what a geographical indication is, how Europe splits them into two levels, PDO and PGI, and the traditional words used for them in France, Italy, Spain and Germany. Then we finish with a handful of terms linked to the vineyard: old vines, vintage, late harvest, noble rot and icewine.

Let's start with the key idea. Where grapes grow influences the style of a wine, so the place of origin appears on labels everywhere in the world. A legally defined vineyard area is called a geographical indication, or GI for short. A GI can be huge, covering a whole region or even a whole country, or tiny, no bigger than a single vineyard. Not every wine comes from a GI, but some statement of origin is always required by law, such as the country where the wine was made.

Outside the European Union, a GI mostly tells you one thing: where the grapes were grown. Growers are free to plant whatever they think will succeed, and there are very few rules about how they grow grapes or make wine. So the styles within one GI can be very different. To guess what is in the bottle, you need another clue, usually the grape variety, which these wines commonly show on the label. South Eastern Australia, for instance, is an Australian GI that covers a vast area.

Inside the European Union, a GI is much more than an address. Each one comes with extra rules that can say which grapes may be planted and how the wine must be made. That is why a European place name is a fairly reliable guide to style. A bottle of Chablis, for example, comes from a GI in France where the rules say the wine must be made from Chardonnay. Often the grape is not even named on the label, because the place name already tells you.

European GIs come in two levels. The first is PDO, which stands for Protected Designation of Origin. PDOs usually cover relatively small areas, with tightly defined rules, and many of Europe's most famous and prestigious wines belong here. The second is PGI, Protected Geographical Indication. PGIs usually cover much wider areas with looser rules, so producers have more freedom in the grapes they plant and the techniques they use. PGI wines range from large-volume, inexpensive, everyday bottles to small-production wines of outstanding quality.

Each country has its own traditional words for these two levels, and the exam expects you to match them. Let's go country by country. In France, a PDO wine carries Appellation d'Origine Protégée, or the older and still very common Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée, often shortened on the label to AOP and AOC. The French term for PGI is Indication Géographique Protégée, or IGP. On a Chablis label you would read Appellation Chablis Contrôlée, with the place name tucked into the middle of the phrase.

In Italy, PDO has two terms. Denominazione di Origine Controllata, or DOC, and the higher level, Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita, or DOCG, where that final G means guaranteed. The Italian PGI term is Indicazione Geografica Tipica, or IGT. In Spain, too, PDO has two terms: Denominación de Origen, DO, and Denominación de Origen Calificada, DOCa, the qualified top level. The Spanish PGI is called Vino de la Tierra, literally wine of the land.

And Germany. Here PDO is shown by Qualitätswein, meaning quality wine, and Prädikatswein, meaning wine with a special attribute; Prädikatswein is the category behind Germany's famous ripeness levels, which we meet with Riesling. The German PGI term is Landwein, country wine. A memory trick for all four countries: PGI always has just one term, IGP, IGT, Vino de la Tierra, Landwein, while PDO usually has two: AOP and AOC, DOC and DOCG, DO and DOCa, Qualitätswein and Prädikatswein.

Now the terms linked to the vineyard. The first is old vines, vieilles vignes in French. Older vines usually produce fewer grapes, and a smaller crop can give grapes with more concentrated and complex aromas, which can lead to better wines. That is why old vines are so prized. But be careful: the term has no legal definition, so how old is old can be argued over, and producers do not always agree.

The vintage is the year the grapes were harvested. It helps you decide when to drink a wine. Most wines are best young, so the vintage tells you how old the wine is and whether it might be past its best. Some wines are made to improve with years in bottle, and then the vintage hints at whether the wine is near its peak. In regions where the weather changes a lot from year to year, the vintage also signals differences in quality and style, which matters most for expensive wines from prestigious regions.

A clever detail about vintages: always check the hemisphere. In the southern hemisphere the harvest happens around March and April, while in the northern hemisphere it comes around September and October. So an Australian wine labelled with a given year is about half a year older than a Californian wine with the same year on the label.

Three last terms point to concentrated grapes. Late harvest means grapes left on the vine and picked well after the usual time, with riper flavours and more sugar. These wines are fuller-bodied and more concentrated, and here is the trap: they can be dry, off-dry, medium or sweet. Botrytis, or noble rot, on a label means the grapes were concentrated by the noble fungus, and these wines are nearly always sweet. Icewine, Eiswein in German, means grapes frozen on the vine and pressed while frozen, giving a juice rich in sugar and acid, often made into sweet wines.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, a GI is a legally defined vineyard area; outside Europe it mostly states where the grapes grew, so look at the grape variety, while inside Europe it also brings rules on grapes and winemaking. Second, PDO means smaller areas and stricter rules, PGI wider areas and more freedom, with these terms: AOP or AOC and IGP in France, DOCG or DOC and IGT in Italy, DOCa or DO and Vino de la Tierra in Spain, Prädikatswein or Qualitätswein and Landwein in Germany. Third, old vines is not legally defined, the vintage is the harvest year, late harvest can be dry or sweet, while noble rot and icewine nearly always mean sweet.

In this lesson we walk into the winery and watch grape juice become wine. We start with alcoholic fermentation, the one step every wine shares. Then we follow the basic stages, from crushing to packaging, and see how they are arranged to make white, rosé and red wines. After that we look at the small adjustments a winemaker can make, at why fermentation temperature matters, and finally at the different ways of making a wine that is not dry but sweet.

First, fermentation. The obvious difference between grape juice and wine is alcohol, and the alcohol comes from tiny living organisms called yeast. Yeast feed on the sugar in the juice and turn it into alcohol. Along the way they also produce carbon dioxide, a gas that is allowed to escape into the air, and heat. Usually fermentation stops on its own when the yeast have eaten all the sugar, and the result is a dry wine. The riper the grapes, the more sugar there is, and the more alcohol the wine will have. Most dry wines end up between eleven and a half and sixteen percent alcohol by volume.

Now the basic steps. Crushing splits the grape skins to release some of the juice. Pressing squeezes the crushed grapes in a machine called a press, to get out as much liquid as possible; depending on the wine, this happens before or after fermentation. After fermentation comes storage. For most wines it is short, less than a year and sometimes only a few months, and the flavours hardly change. Some wines, though, are kept much longer. We call this maturation, and it usually happens in oak, which can add flavours of its own.

During a long maturation, the wine slowly evolves: fresh primary fruit gives way to tertiary aromas, and structural parts such as tannin become more integrated. The last step is packaging. Glass bottles remain by far the most popular choice, but wine is also sold in bag-in-box, plastic bottles and cartons.

Let's put the steps in order for a white wine. White wine is usually made from white grapes. The grapes are crushed and then pressed straight away, before fermentation, and the skins are normally thrown away. Only the juice ferments. Then comes storage or maturation, and finally packaging. Here is a reminder from our first lesson: since colour is only in the skins, black grapes can also make a white wine, as long as they are pressed very gently and the juice leaves the skins quickly.

For a red wine, the order changes. Red wine must be made from black grapes, and the skins must stay in the fermenting juice, because that is where colour and tannin come from. So the grapes are crushed and then fermented with their skins. When fermentation is over, the new wine is drained off the skins, and the skins are pressed to squeeze out the wine still trapped in them. Then come storage or maturation, and packaging. In short: white wines are pressed before fermentation, red wines after.

Extracting colour and tannin needs some help. The heat of fermentation helps, but it is not enough, because the skins float to the top of the tank and form a thick layer called the cap. Left alone, the cap gives up little colour or tannin. So the skins must be mixed with the liquid often and thoroughly. Two common techniques are punching down, where a plunger pushes the cap down into the liquid, and pumping over, where juice from the bottom of the tank is pumped up through a hose and sprayed over the cap.

And rosé? There are two common methods. The first is short maceration. Black grapes start fermenting exactly as for a red wine, but after only a few hours the juice is drained off the skins. It has just a little colour, and it finishes fermenting like a white wine. The second method is blending: mixing a red wine with a white wine. Be careful, this is not allowed in many parts of Europe. And rosé is rarely matured in oak.

Next, temperature. Fermentation creates heat, so winemakers watch it closely and today can chill or warm their tanks. Red wines ferment warmer, from about twenty to thirty-two degrees Celsius, because heat helps extract colour and tannin from the skins. White wines ferment cooler, from about twelve to twenty-two degrees, and at the cool end fermentation can create notably fruity aromas. A rosé made by short maceration, once off the skins, ferments at white wine temperatures.

Sometimes the grapes are not quite in balance, so winemakers can make small adjustments. In cool climates or cool years, the grapes may lack sugar, giving wines that are low in alcohol and light in body; the winemaker can raise the sugar level in the juice, so the wine gains alcohol. In warm climates, acidity can fall too low and the wine would taste flat, so acid can be added. In cool climates the opposite can happen, and some of the acid can be neutralised.

Finally, sweet wines. Sugar left in a wine after fermentation is called residual sugar, and the amount varies from a touch in off-dry wines to a lot in sweet wines. There are four main techniques. The first uses grapes with concentrated sugar, from extra-ripe, noble-rotted or frozen fruit: there is so much sugar that the yeast cannot eat it all and fermentation stops with sugar left over. Tokaji Aszú from Hungary is made this way.

The second technique removes the yeast with extremely fine filters, which stops fermentation; White Zinfandel from California is an example. The third kills the yeast by adding alcohol to the fermenting juice. This is fortification. It raises the strength to between fifteen and twenty percent, the yeast die before finishing the sugar, and the wine cannot start fermenting again. Port is the classic example. The fourth, very common, adds sweetness to a dry wine, using unfermented grape juice, concentrated grape juice, or a sweet wine. Winemakers like it because they can control the sweetness precisely.

A memory tip for the order of the steps: for white, think "press, then party"; the juice is pressed first and the yeast party comes after. For red, think "party, then press"; the yeast party happens with the skins in the room, and the pressing comes at the end.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, yeast turn sugar into alcohol, carbon dioxide and heat, and when all the sugar is gone the wine is dry. Second, whites are pressed before fermentation and ferment cool, at twelve to twenty-two degrees, reds ferment on their skins at twenty to thirty-two degrees with punching down or pumping over and are pressed afterwards, and rosé comes from a short maceration or, outside much of Europe, from blending. Third, sweet wines come from concentrated grapes, from removing the yeast, from fortification, or from adding sweetness to a dry wine.

In the last lesson we followed the basic path from grape to wine. In this lesson we look at the choices that give a wine its personality. We start with the vessels a wine is made and stored in: stainless steel, concrete and oak. We spend some time on oak, because new or old, small or large, and the level of toast all change the result. Then we meet malolactic conversion, lees and blending, and we finish with what happens to red and white wines as they age in the bottle.

First, the vessels. Winemakers use tanks and barrels of many shapes and sizes, but the easiest way to sort them is into two groups: inert vessels and oak. Stainless steel and concrete are inert, which means they add no flavour at all. They can be used for fermentation and for storage, and they can be made airtight, so no oxygen reaches the wine. That keeps the fresh, fruity flavours of the grape intact. Think of a crisp, aromatic white: it has very likely spent its life in stainless steel.

Oak is different. Most wooden vessels are made of oak, and they too can be used for fermentation or storage. A winemaker chooses oak for two reasons. First, it can give flavours directly to the wine. Second, it lets the wine slowly meet oxygen during maturation, which makes its flavours evolve. So oak is both an ingredient and a slow breathing space.

How much flavour does a barrel give? That depends on how it was made, and on its age and size. When a barrel is built, the oak staves are heated over an open flame to bend them into shape. How long and how strongly they are heated is called the toast. Toasting brings sweet-spice and charred wood aromas. Then age. A brand-new barrel, called new oak, gives a lot of flavour: vanilla, coconut, charred wood, spice. Each time a barrel is reused it gives less, and after two or three uses there is very little flavour left. Used barrels are called old oak.

Barrels are watertight, but not airtight. During maturation a little oxygen enters and works on the wine. This can bring flavours such as caramel, dried fruit and nuts, like hazelnut, almond and walnut, and it softens the tannins of red wines. Size matters here. In a small barrel more of the wine touches the wood, so these changes happen faster. Large oak vessels act more slowly, and they are rarely used to add oak flavour at all.

Oak barrels are expensive. For less expensive wines there is a cheaper shortcut: oak staves or oak chips, added to wine sitting in an inert tank. They give oak flavour at a fraction of the cost, though without the slow oxygen effect of a barrel. A simple picture: new oak is a strong cup of tea from a fresh tea bag, old oak is the same bag used for the third time, and chips are like adding a spoonful of flavouring.

Now malolactic conversion. It takes place after alcoholic fermentation, and it is not done by yeast but by a different microorganism: bacteria. It lowers the acidity of the wine and can add buttery flavours. In red wines it nearly always happens, and the buttery notes are hardly noticeable. In white wines it is a choice. For aromatic grapes like Riesling, winemakers usually prevent it, to keep fresh acidity and pure fruit. For some styles of Chardonnay, they welcome it, for a softer, creamier wine.

Then the lees. After fermentation the yeast die and sink to the bottom of the vessel as a layer of dead cells called lees. With white wines, the winemaker can choose to leave the wine in contact with them, and even to stir them up through the wine during maturation. This adds body and brings flavours of biscuit and bread. If you meet a white wine that feels round and tastes faintly of fresh bread, lees may be the reason.

Blending can happen at many stages and shapes the style of a wine. There are two main reasons. The first is consistency: people expect some branded wines to taste the same every year, so the winemaker blends different wines each vintage to keep that style. The second is complexity: wines from different grapes, different vineyards or different techniques can be combined into something more interesting than any of its parts.

Before bottling, most wines are also clarified, for example by filtering, because most people expect a perfectly clear wine. Some producers skip filtering to protect character, so their wines may look slightly less bright.

Last, ageing in the bottle. Here is a surprise for many: most wines do not improve in the bottle. Their fruit fades and is replaced by vegetal notes, so they are best drunk young. Only some wines can improve over years or even decades. They usually have high acidity; sweet wines have high sugar, red wines high tannin, and these act as preservatives. But above all, they need enough concentration of flavour to evolve in a positive way. Fresh fruit turns into dried fruit, and complex notes such as mushroom and leather appear.

What do we see and taste? A white wine changes colour from lemon to gold to amber, and its colour becomes deeper. Tertiary notes such as dried apricot, honey, nuts and spice develop. A red wine goes the other way in intensity: from ruby to garnet to tawny and eventually brown, becoming paler. Its tannins grow softer and smoother, and notes like fig, prune, meat and wet leaves appear. Old reds often throw a deposit in the bottle, and if there is a lot of it, the wine is usually decanted before serving.

A memory tip for bottle ageing: whites darken, reds fade. A white wine moves towards gold and amber, getting deeper, while a red wine loses its colour towards brick and brown, getting paler. If you remember that the two colours walk towards each other over time, you will not mix them up.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, stainless steel and concrete are inert and can be airtight, keeping fruit fresh, while oak adds flavour and lets in oxygen; new oak and small barrels work fastest and strongest, toasting adds spice and charred notes, and after two or three uses a barrel gives little flavour. Second, malolactic conversion is done by bacteria, lowers acidity and can add butter, nearly always in reds and by choice in whites, lees add body and bread or biscuit notes, and blending brings consistency and complexity. Third, most wines do not improve in bottle, and those that do need acidity, sugar or tannin and, above all, concentration; whites deepen from lemon to amber, reds fade from ruby to brown.

Welcome to the first of the great international grapes: Chardonnay. If one white grape could be called a chameleon, it is this one. It makes outstanding wines in cool, moderate and warm climates, from simple, inexpensive everyday bottles to some of the most sought-after whites in the world, able to age for years. In this lesson we see how climate changes its flavours, which winemaking choices shape it, and then we tour its key regions, from Burgundy to the New World.

Let's start with climate, because with Chardonnay it changes almost everything: the fruit, the alcohol, the body and the acidity. A cool-climate Chardonnay has high acidity, a light to medium body and flavours of green fruit like apple and pear, citrus like lemon, and a mineral note of wet stones. In a moderate climate it gains medium to high acidity, a medium to full body and flavours of lemon, peach and sometimes melon. In a warm climate it is full-bodied, with medium acidity, and tastes mostly of peach and tropical fruit like pineapple and banana.

Chardonnay is also a winemaker's grape that welcomes secondary flavours. Malolactic conversion softens sharp acidity and adds butter and cream. Lees contact adds body and notes of bread and biscuit. Oak barrels add body and smoke, vanilla and coconut, while cheaper wines may use oak chips or staves. In warm regions, acid is often added for balance. But all of these are options: only wines with enough flavour intensity benefit, and some producers choose inert vessels for a pure, unoaked or unwooded style. The very best Chardonnays can age for years, gaining notes of hazelnut and mushroom.

Burgundy, in France, is Chardonnay's home. It stretches from cool Chablis in the north, through the moderate Côte d'Or, down to the Mâconnais in the south. Wines labelled with the regional appellation Bourgogne can come from anywhere in the region and are usually simple, with apple, lemon and high acidity. Chablis, a village appellation, is cool. Its wines are dry, light to medium in body, with high acidity and apple, lemon and wet-stone flavours. Producers almost always ferment in inert vessels to protect that delicate fruit, so oak is rarely noticeable.

The best Chablis vineyards, labelled Premier Cru or Grand Cru, lie on hillsides facing south or south-west, catching more sun and giving riper, more complex wines. Frost is the big worry in this cool place and can cut the size of the crop. Further south, in the Côte d'Or, the climate is moderate and the wines have more body and riper fruit, like peach and melon. Chardonnay is focused south of the town of Beaune, in the Côte de Beaune, where the villages of Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet make very good to outstanding wines.

These wines are often fermented or matured in oak and aged on their lees for complexity and body. The premier cru and grand cru vineyards of these villages can develop hazelnut and mushroom notes for decades, and many consider them the peak of Chardonnay worldwide, with prices to match. In the south, the Mâconnais gives fruity, mostly unoaked wines labelled Mâcon, with simple lemon, peach and melon flavours. Around the village of Pouilly-Fuissé, steep slopes facing east and south-east give richer wines with concentrated stone and tropical fruit, often fermented or matured in oak.

Still in France, the Languedoc-Roussillon runs along the Mediterranean coast. Most of its Chardonnay is labelled Pays d'Oc IGP. The climate is warm, and large volumes of ripe, fruity wine are made, with peach, pineapple and banana. The best may be fermented or matured in barrels, while inexpensive branded wines more often use oak chips or staves.

Now the United States. In California, Chardonnay is everywhere and covers every quality level. The inland Central Valley is very warm and dry, cut off from the sea by mountains, and irrigation allows high yields. These grapes go into high-volume wines simply labelled California, with peach and pineapple, medium acidity and medium body, and any oak usually comes from chips or staves. Closer to the coast, cooler influences slow ripening and give intense, balanced wines: Los Carneros is cooled by morning fogs from San Pablo Bay, and coastal Sonoma by Pacific breezes.

Napa Valley grows warmer and sunnier as you head north, and it is known for full-bodied Chardonnay with pronounced tropical fruit and vanilla and spice from new oak. On the Central Coast, Santa Barbara County gets sea breezes funnelled inland by valleys that run east to west, and its styles range from wines close to the Côte de Beaune to riper, tropical, new-oaked wines. Further north, Oregon has a mostly moderate climate and smaller production, with refreshingly high acidity and flavours from lemon to melon.

Next, the southern hemisphere. In Australia, high-volume wines labelled South Eastern Australia can come from a huge area, often warm, irrigated inland vineyards, and are sometimes blended with Semillon or with cooler-climate wine for balance. Adelaide Hills is cooled by altitude and the Yarra Valley by southern ocean currents, giving peach and sometimes tropical fruit, medium to high acidity and carefully balanced oak. Margaret River, in Western Australia, is warm but cooled by sea breezes, and makes consistently high-quality, medium to full-bodied wines with peach and pineapple.

In New Zealand, Marlborough, at the north-east tip of the South Island, is cool but sunny, with sea breezes and plenty of rain. Its Chardonnay shows ripe lemon, peach and melon, high natural acidity and subtle oak. Hawke's Bay, on the east coast of the North Island, is moderate, and Chardonnay is its most planted white grape: full-bodied wines with high acidity and pronounced stone fruit. In Chile, the coastal Casablanca Valley is cooled by Pacific breezes and morning fogs, giving refreshing lemon and peach wines, while the larger, warmer Central Valley ranges from inexpensive brands to outstanding wines from higher, cooler vineyards.

In South Africa, the hot inland vineyards of the Western Cape mostly make high-volume branded wines, sometimes blending Chardonnay with Chenin Blanc. Walker Bay, on the coast, is one of the country's coolest areas thanks to strong southern sea breezes, and it is known for very good Chardonnay with high acidity, peach, pineapple and oak. Today, after a fashion for heavy oak in the past, the trend is to let the fruit speak, and the steady popularity of Chablis owes something to its unoaked style.

A memory tip: think of Chardonnay as a fruit bowl that moves with the sun. Cool regions like Chablis fill it with apples and lemons. Moderate regions like the Côte de Beaune add peaches. Warm regions like Pays d'Oc or California's Central Valley pile on pineapple and banana.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, the climate sets the fruit: green and citrus in cool regions, stone fruit in moderate ones, tropical fruit in warm ones, with acidity falling and body rising as it gets warmer. Second, malolactic conversion, lees and oak are common but optional, and only flavour-intense wines benefit from them. Third, in Burgundy, Chablis is cool and unoaked, Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet are oaked and age-worthy, and Mâcon and Pouilly-Fuissé are in the south, while fogs, breezes and altitude make cooler, fresher styles in regions like Los Carneros, Sonoma, Casablanca, Adelaide Hills, Yarra Valley and Walker Bay.

In this lesson we meet a grape you can often recognise with your eyes closed: Sauvignon Blanc. Open a glass and the aromas leap out: freshly cut grass, green pepper, a squeeze of grapefruit. In this lesson we look at what makes the grape so distinctive, how it is usually made, and why it is best drunk young. Then we travel from its French homes in the Loire and Bordeaux to New Zealand, Australia, Chile, South Africa and California.

First, the grape. Sauvignon Blanc is an aromatic white variety, French in origin and now grown around the world, and it does best in cool and moderate climates. It usually makes dry wines with a light to medium body and refreshing high acidity. Its signature is a set of pronounced herbaceous aromas: grass, green bell pepper and asparagus. Alongside those, the fruit depends on ripeness. Less ripe grapes give green fruit like apple and gooseberry, citrus like grapefruit, and wet stones. Riper grapes give stone fruit like peach and tropical fruit like passion fruit.

That range of ripeness is a tool. By blending grapes from different vineyards, picked at different levels of ripeness, a winemaker can build a wine that shows both the green, zesty side and the riper, tropical side at once, gaining complexity. Sauvignon Blanc is usually a single-varietal wine, but it is sometimes blended with Semillon, a partnership we will meet in Bordeaux and Australia.

In the winery, most Sauvignon Blanc is made in inert vessels like stainless steel. The reason is simple: those vivid herbaceous aromas are easily drowned by the flavours of new oak. When oak is used, the label often says so, with words such as barrel aged. And here is a key point for the exam: Sauvignon Blanc is usually best drunk young. Even outstanding examples can lose their fresh aromas within a couple of years of the vintage and develop unattractive vegetal notes.

Let's begin in France, in the Loire Valley. Two appellations sit facing each other across the River Loire: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé. In both, Sauvignon Blanc is the only white grape allowed. The climate is cool, and the wines are dry and high in acidity, with green apple, herbaceous notes of grass and asparagus, and sometimes a wet-stone character. Further west, the wider Touraine area makes Sauvignon Blanc labelled Touraine: typically fruity and inexpensive.

In Bordeaux, Sauvignon Blanc makes a wide range of styles. Simple wines labelled Bordeaux have fresh aromas of grass and green apple, and can be pure Sauvignon Blanc or a blend with Semillon. The wines of Graves and Pessac-Léognan are more concentrated and complex, and usually blend the two grapes. Semillon adds body and helps the wine age. The very good and outstanding wines from these two appellations are often matured in oak and develop complex notes of honey and nuts in the bottle: the exception to the drink-young rule.

Still in France, most of the Languedoc-Roussillon is too warm for Sauvignon Blanc. The best wines come from vineyards cooled by altitude. A typical example is dry and high in acidity, with passion fruit and a grassy note, and it is usually labelled Pays d'Oc IGP.

Now New Zealand, and the region that made Sauvignon Blanc world famous: Marlborough, in the north-east of the South Island. The climate is cool, and the wines are typically more pronounced than those of the Loire. Producers often blend grapes from different sites or picked at different ripeness levels, so the wines can show grapefruit, peach and passion fruit together with intense green pepper and asparagus. Some producers are now exploring beyond the classic style: grapes from cooler sites for a Loire-like wine, or small amounts of oak or lees contact for complexity and body.

In Australia, Margaret River in Western Australia is known for Sauvignon Blanc, most often blended with Semillon. These wines show concentrated grassy aromas, and some see oak. In the Adelaide Hills of South Australia, cooled by altitude, Sauvignon Blanc is the most planted grape of all. Most wines are fresh and fruity, from citrus to tropical fruit, and some are blended with Semillon for a fuller body and longer life.

In Chile, the coastal Casablanca Valley is cooled by sea breezes and morning fogs, and has a firm reputation for very good Sauvignon Blanc. The larger Central Valley makes everything from inexpensive high-volume brands to very good examples. In South Africa, inland areas are generally too warm, so Sauvignon Blanc is mostly grown near the coast. Constantia, south of Cape Town, is cooled by breezes from the Southern Ocean and makes refreshing wines with ripe tropical fruit and herbaceous notes. Elgin, cooled by altitude and often called the country's coolest region, gives green apple and sometimes wet-stone aromas.

Finally, California. Most of it is too warm for the fresh, herbaceous style of France and New Zealand. The best grapes come from cooler spots and may be picked early to keep their acidity and green aromas. Very good examples of this style come from the cooler parts of Napa Valley, and they are sometimes made with oak to add body and a smoky note.

Sauvignon Blanc is hugely popular today. Like a trusted brand, its flavours are distinctive and easy to recognise, and it is refreshing with or without food. Some producers worry that drinkers may one day tire of such intense green aromas, which is why they are experimenting beyond the classic style.

A memory tip: think of Sauvignon Blanc as a walk through a vegetable garden next to an orchard. In the cooler corners, like Sancerre, Pouilly-Fumé or Elgin, you smell cut grass, asparagus and green apple. Step into the sunnier orchard, like Marlborough's riper sites or Constantia, and passion fruit and peach join in. And remember: it is best picked, and drunk, fresh.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Sauvignon Blanc is an aromatic grape for cool and moderate climates, giving dry, light to medium-bodied wines with high acidity and pronounced grass, green pepper and asparagus aromas, with fruit from green and citrus to tropical as ripeness rises. Second, it is usually made in inert vessels and drunk young, except for the oaked Sauvignon Blanc and Semillon blends of Graves and Pessac-Léognan, which can age. Third, Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé are the cool Loire classics, Marlborough is more pronounced, and cool sites such as Adelaide Hills, Casablanca, Elgin, Constantia and cooler parts of Napa make fresh styles elsewhere.

In this lesson we meet a grape that many wine professionals call their favourite: Riesling. It can make a feather-light wine with a touch of sweetness, a bone-dry wine that tastes like lime and stones, or a rich, honeyed dessert wine that lives for decades. We will see what makes the grape special, how winemakers create its different levels of sweetness, and then we visit its key regions: the Mosel, Rheingau and Pfalz in Germany, Alsace in France, and the Clare and Eden Valleys in Australia.

First, the grape. Riesling is a cold-hardy white variety that likes cool to moderate climates. It is aromatic, with pronounced fruity and floral aromas, and it has naturally high acidity. Its fruit depends on ripeness at harvest. Just-ripe grapes give green fruit like apple and pear, citrus like lemon and lime, and blossom. Extra-ripe grapes give stone fruit like peach and apricot, tropical fruit like mango and pineapple, and sometimes even dried apricot.

Two features make Riesling perfect for sweet wines. It keeps its acidity while slowly building up sugar and flavour, so it can be left on the vine for a late harvest where autumns are dry and sunny. And it is susceptible to noble rot. Sugar can also be concentrated by freezing the grapes on the vine. Whatever the route, Riesling's high acidity is the perfect counterweight to sweetness: it stops a sweet wine from tasting heavy or sticky.

So Riesling comes in every style: dry, off-dry, medium and sweet, light to full in body. How are the in-between styles made? Off-dry and medium wines are usually made by stopping fermentation by removing the yeast, which leaves lower alcohol and some sugar, or by adding unfermented grape juice to a dry wine; the German name for that juice is Süssreserve. The sweetest wines come from extra-ripe grapes so rich in sugar that fermentation stops by itself.

In the winery, Riesling is usually fermented in inert vessels such as stainless steel, to protect its floral aromas. It usually avoids malolactic conversion too, to keep its fresh acidity. The finest Rieslings can age for years or even decades. Their acidity keeps them tasting fresh while they develop tertiary notes of honey and a curious, very typical aroma of petrol.

Now Germany, Riesling's heartland. The climate is mostly cool, with some vineyards beyond fifty degrees north, and Riesling is the most important grape, planted throughout the country. The Mosel is one of the most northerly regions. Its Rieslings are lighter in body than those from further south, and often have medium sweetness to balance very high acidity. The best vineyards sit on steep slopes facing south or south-west above the river, where the sun-facing aspect, stony soils and sunlight reflected off the water all help the grapes ripen.

The Rheingau has its vineyards on steep south-facing slopes on the north bank of the Rhine, to catch as much sun and warmth as possible. Its wines are usually drier and fuller in body than those of the Mosel. The Pfalz, near the French border, is sheltered by mountains to the west and is dry and sunny. In climate it is almost an extension of Alsace, and a typical Pfalz Riesling is dry and medium-bodied.

German labels often talk about ripeness, because in a cool country ripeness cannot be taken for granted. Landwein is the PGI level, usually light and dry to off-dry. Qualitätswein must come from one of thirteen wine-growing areas, such as the Mosel or Rheingau, with riper grapes. Prädikatswein needs riper grapes still, from a single area, and has six categories based on sugar at harvest. Kabinett is the lightest and most delicate. Spätlese, meaning late harvest, is riper and fuller. Auslese, from selected extra-ripe bunches, brings stone, tropical and dried fruit. These three can be sweet or dry, and a dry Auslese has more alcohol than a dry Kabinett.

The three top categories are always sweet, because the sugar must be concentrated on the vine. Beerenauslese, or BA, comes from berries concentrated by noble rot, with apricot, mango, dried fruit and honey. Trockenbeerenauslese, or TBA, uses individually picked berries shrivelled by noble rot, and is rarer and even more intense. Eiswein comes from grapes frozen on the vine, with no noble rot at all, and vibrant peach, apricot and pineapple. These wines are low in alcohol, age for decades, and are made in tiny quantities. Where sweetness is unclear, labels may add trocken for dry, or halbtrocken for a wine with some sweetness.

Now France. Alsace lies east of the Vosges Mountains, which block the rain-bearing westerly winds, making it one of the driest and sunniest regions in France. The best vineyards are in the foothills, facing east or south-east to catch the morning sun, and dry autumns stretch out the ripening season. A typical Alsace Riesling is dry, with pronounced intensity, ripe citrus and stone fruit, a medium body and high acidity. The best come from single vineyards called grands crus, and sweeter wines from late-picked grapes are labelled Vendanges Tardives.

Finally, Australia, where Riesling has been grown since the early nineteenth century. Premium Riesling is centred on two regions in South Australia: the Clare Valley and the Eden Valley. Their altitude gives them a moderate climate, unlike the warm Barossa Valley next door. They make refreshing, dry Rieslings with pronounced lime and lemon and, sometimes, that petrol note. Beyond these places, Riesling shines wherever it is cool, dry and sunny enough for its sugars and flavours to develop slowly.

A memory tip: think of Riesling as a tightrope walker, with acidity as the balancing pole. Because the pole is so long, Riesling can carry anything, from a dry wine with nothing in its hands to a huge, sweet load like a Trockenbeerenauslese, without ever falling into heaviness. And the walk can go on for decades.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Riesling is an aromatic, high-acid grape for cool and moderate climates; it is fermented in inert vessels, comes in every style from dry to sweet, and the best age for decades, gaining honey and petrol notes. Second, in Germany the Mosel is light with medium sweetness and very high acidity, the Rheingau drier and fuller, the Pfalz dry and medium-bodied, and Prädikatswein ranges from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese and Eiswein. Third, Alsace Riesling is dry, pronounced and medium-bodied, and the Clare and Eden Valleys make dry, lime-scented Riesling cooled by altitude.

In this lesson we meet one grape with two names and two personalities: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris. Pinot Grigio is the Italian name, Pinot Gris the French one, but it is exactly the same variety. What makes this lesson so useful is that it shows, more clearly than almost any other grape, how decisions in the vineyard, yield and harvest date, can create two completely different wines. We will look at both styles, at how they are made, and then at their homes in Italy and in Alsace.

First, the grape. Pinot Grigio or Pinot Gris is a white variety that grows mainly in cool and moderate climates. Its skin often has a pinkish-grey tint, which is where the name grey Pinot comes from. It is very versatile in the vineyard, and the grower's choices decide which of its two faces we will see in the glass.

The first face, and by far the most common, is the light style. Here the vines are allowed to give high yields, and the grapes are picked early to keep their acidity. The result is a dry, light-bodied wine with medium to high acidity and simple flavours of pear and lemon. It is easy, refreshing and usually inexpensive. Think of it as a crisp glass for a sunny terrace, not a wine to ponder over.

The second face is very different. Yields are kept low and the harvest is delayed. These riper grapes have more sugar, less acidity and more complex flavours. From them, winemakers can make a powerful, full-bodied wine with medium acidity and pronounced flavours of lemon, peach and tropical fruit like mango and banana. Same grape, same vine: only the yield and the picking date have changed. That is the key lesson.

In the winery, both styles are usually fermented in inert vessels, to keep the fruit fresh and clean. The light Italian style is almost always fermented until it is completely dry. Producers of the riper, fuller style sometimes stop the fermentation by removing the yeast, to keep an off-dry or medium level of sweetness. Ageing also differs. Light Pinot Grigio is best drunk young and fresh, because its simple flavours fade quickly in the bottle. The more concentrated, full-bodied wines can develop notes of ginger and honey over time.

Now the regions, starting in Italy. With few exceptions, Italian Pinot Grigio is simple, unoaked and light in body. Much of it comes from the Veneto, in the north-east of the country, and is labelled either delle Venezie DOC or Veneto IGT. Because it is made in huge volumes, it is usually inexpensive, with a short finish, and its quality is most often acceptable to good.

There is a more ambitious side to Italy too. In Friuli-Venezia Giulia, in the far north-eastern corner of the country, producers make a more complex, fuller-bodied Pinot Grigio. If the Veneto version is a simple sketch, Friuli adds more colour and detail to the picture.

Now France, and Alsace, where the grape goes by the name Pinot Gris. Here it is usually picked later in the season, when the grapes are extra-ripe. By then, acidity has fallen to medium, while sugar and flavour complexity have grown. Depending on the producer, the wines range from dry to medium-sweet. They are typically medium to full in body, with pronounced peach and mango, and they can develop honey and ginger in the bottle.

Alsace has a few label terms worth knowing. Alsace AOC is the regional appellation, and its wines are usually labelled with the grape variety; since the 2021 vintage, the level of sweetness must also be shown on a standard scale. The best Pinot Gris come from the Alsace Grand Cru vineyards, mostly on the steep foothills of the Vosges Mountains, facing east or south-east. These sites get more sun, so the wines are riper and fuller than those from the flatter plain. Pinot Gris shares these grand cru sites with Riesling and Gewurztraminer.

One more Alsace term: Vendanges Tardives, which means late harvest. It usually indicates a medium to sweet wine from extra-ripe grapes, and it can be used for Pinot Gris, Riesling and Gewurztraminer, on both Alsace and Alsace Grand Cru wines.

Pinot Grigio in its lightest form has been a huge success, exported in vast quantities from the Veneto, a sign that many everyday drinkers have moved away from heavy, oaky whites. But that abundance means people looking for intensity often overlook the grape, which is a pity, because the riper styles are complex and pair well with strongly flavoured food. Outside Italy and France, producers often use the names as a style signal: Pinot Grigio for a lighter, higher-acid wine, Pinot Gris for a fuller, more complex one.

A memory tip: Grigio is Italian, light and lean, like a quick espresso at the bar. Gris is French, rich and round, like a long lunch in Alsace. When a label outside Europe says Grigio, expect the espresso; when it says Gris, expect the lunch.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same grape, and its two styles come mainly from yield and harvest date: high yields and early picking give a light, dry wine with pear and lemon, while low yields and late picking give a full-bodied wine with peach and tropical fruit. Second, Italian Pinot Grigio from the Veneto, labelled delle Venezie DOC or Veneto IGT, is light, simple and best young, while Friuli-Venezia Giulia makes a fuller style. Third, Alsace Pinot Gris is extra-ripe, medium to full-bodied, dry to medium-sweet, can gain honey and ginger with age, and is at its best from grand cru sites or as Vendanges Tardives.

In this lesson we meet the most temperamental of the great black grapes: Pinot Noir. It is difficult to grow, it is fussy about climate, and yet its wines are among the most sought after in the world. We will look at the grape and the wines it makes, at how winemakers treat it, and then we follow it from its home in Burgundy to California, Oregon, Chile, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

First, the grape. Pinot Noir is a black variety with a thin skin, and it needs a cool to moderate climate to give good grapes. If it gets too warm, it loses its fresh fruit and tastes unpleasantly cooked. Thin skins also make it prone to rot and disease, so in a poor vintage growers can struggle to make even a small amount of good wine. That is one reason Pinot Noir is rarely inexpensive.

In the glass, Pinot Noir is usually pale to medium in colour. That thin skin means less pigment, so do not expect a deep, inky purple. On the palate it has high acidity and low to medium tannins. The fruit is red: strawberry, raspberry and red cherry, fresh in cooler places and more cooked in riper ones. Most Pinot Noir is fruity and refreshing, and delicious young.

In the winery, Pinot Noir is almost always made as a single-varietal wine, the notable exception being sparkling wines like Champagne, where it is blended. It is often matured in oak, but care is needed: strong flavours from small new barrels can easily drown such a delicate wine. Many producers prefer older or larger barrels, which give less flavour. The best Pinot Noirs show subtle smoke, cloves and vanilla, balanced by the fruit. A few very good and outstanding wines can age for years, gaining forest floor and mushroom notes.

Now Burgundy, Pinot Noir's home. The climate runs from cool in the north to moderate further south, and Pinot Noir does best in the moderate areas where it can ripen fully. In Burgundy, tiny changes in the vineyard really matter. The best sites are on slopes facing south and south-east, catching extra sunshine and giving concentrated, complex wines that can age. The most celebrated vineyards are in the Côte d'Or, which has two halves: the Côte de Nuits in the north and the Côte de Beaune in the south.

Burgundy's appellations form a neat pyramid. At the base is the regional appellation, Bourgogne, covering the whole region. Red Bourgogne is light to medium-bodied, with low tannin, high acidity and fresh red fruit, made to drink young. Because demand for red Burgundy is so high, even simple Bourgogne can be expensive. One level up are the village appellations, usually from better sites, with more intensity, complexity and length. In the Côte de Nuits, think of Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges; in the Côte de Beaune, Beaune and Pommard.

At the top are the premier cru and grand cru vineyards, usually on slopes facing south or south-east. Their wines have concentrated strawberry and red cherry, subtle oak, and develop pronounced forest floor and mushroom with age. A premier cru wine shows the village name with the words Premier Cru, and sometimes the vineyard name. The grands crus are the very best single vineyards, with their own appellations. They are the most concentrated, complex and age-worthy, and, being rare, they command exceptionally high prices.

Now the New World. Some regions there are closer to the equator than Burgundy and should be far too warm, but moderating influences such as fog, sea breezes and ocean currents make great Pinot Noir possible. Much of California is too warm, but a few coastal regions shine. Los Carneros is cooled by morning fogs from San Pablo Bay, the western parts of Sonoma by Pacific breezes, and Santa Barbara County, on the Central Coast, by sea breezes from the west and south. Californian Pinot Noir tends to show ripe strawberry and red cherry, often with notable oak, and the finest develop forest floor and mushroom.

Oregon, further north and exposed to the Pacific, is cooler than California and mostly moderate, ideal for Pinot Noir. Its best wines have complex, fresh red fruit, subtle oak, and gain earthy, mushroomy notes with age. In Chile, the coastal Casablanca Valley, between Santiago and the sea, is cooled by Pacific breezes and morning fogs. Its Pinot Noir shows strawberry and sometimes herbal notes, and offers excellent value for money. In South Africa, Pinot Noir is grown in the coolest coastal areas; in Walker Bay, strong southerly breezes give vibrant red fruit and some very good and outstanding wines.

Australia is mostly warm, but a few places are cool enough. The Yarra Valley and the Mornington Peninsula, both in Victoria, are cooled by breezes from the Southern Ocean. Their wines range from light and fragrant to riper, with cooked red plum and strawberry and medium tannins.

In New Zealand, Pinot Noir is the leading black grape. The cool climates of Martinborough, in the North Island, and Marlborough both make very good and outstanding examples. Then there is Central Otago, the surprise. Despite being so far south, it makes the country's ripest, most powerful Pinot Noir. A ring of mountains shelters it from sea breezes and rain, so the vines enjoy intensely sunny days and cool nights. The wines show pronounced strawberry and red cherry, medium to full body and medium tannins; they are often oak-aged and may need a few years in bottle.

Pinot Noir is famous for expressing tiny differences between vineyards: Burgundy lovers claim they can taste the difference between plots a few metres apart. Its popularity has also pushed it into regions that are too warm, giving alcoholic wines without the grape's fresh fruit. That contrast shows how important it is to match a grape with the right climate.

A memory tip: think of Pinot Noir as a ballet dancer. It is light on its feet, pale in colour, with fine tannins and lively acidity. It hates heat, it is fragile and easily hurt by rot, and it needs a gentle hand in the winery, older or larger barrels rather than heavy new oak. But when everything is right, its performance is unforgettable.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Pinot Noir is a thin-skinned black grape for cool to moderate climates, prone to rot, giving pale to medium-coloured wines with high acidity, low to medium tannins and red fruit, often matured in older or larger oak. Second, in Burgundy the best wines come from the Côte d'Or, split into Côte de Nuits, with Gevrey-Chambertin and Nuits-Saint-Georges, and Côte de Beaune, with Beaune and Pommard, rising from Bourgogne to village, premier cru and grand cru. Third, elsewhere it relies on cooling influences, in Los Carneros, Sonoma, Santa Barbara, Oregon, Casablanca, Walker Bay, Yarra Valley, Mornington Peninsula, Martinborough and Marlborough, while sheltered, sunny Central Otago makes New Zealand's ripest style.

In this lesson we meet one of the most famous red grapes on the planet: Cabernet Sauvignon. It is the backbone of the great wines of Bordeaux's Left Bank, and today outstanding examples come from almost every wine country. We will look at what the grape is like, why it so often spends time in oak and why it can age for decades. Then we tour its key regions: Bordeaux and the Languedoc in France, Napa Valley and Sonoma in California, Chile, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

First, the grape. Cabernet Sauvignon is a black variety from south-west France. Its grapes are small, with thick skins full of colour, flavour and tannin. It needs a long, warm growing season to ripen fully, so it grows in moderate and warm climates; in a moderate climate it can struggle to ripen except in the warmest sites. A single-varietal Cabernet Sauvignon is deeply coloured, dry, high in acidity, high in tannin and medium to full in body. Its signature is pronounced black fruit, blackcurrant and black cherry, usually with a herbal note of mint or a herbaceous note of green bell pepper. In very warm places the fruit can taste cooked.

In the winery, Cabernet Sauvignon is often blended, especially with Merlot. Merlot's softer, fleshier fruit fills in around Cabernet's firm structure and tames its very high tannin and acidity. This matters most in cooler years in moderate climates, when Cabernet may not ripen fully. Think of Cabernet Sauvignon as the frame of a house and Merlot as the furniture that makes it comfortable.

A freshly fermented Cabernet Sauvignon can taste harshly tannic. So it usually spends months or even years in oak barrels before bottling. The small amount of oxygen that passes through the barrel helps soften the tannins, and new oak adds secondary flavours of smoke, vanilla, cloves and cedar. Then comes the bottle. High tannin and acidity act as natural preservatives, so very good and outstanding wines can mature for many years. Over time the tannins soften and tertiary notes appear: dried fruit, earth and forest floor.

Now Bordeaux. The climate is moderate and maritime, and in its coolest sites Cabernet Sauvignon may not ripen reliably. The secret of the Left Bank, west and south of the Gironde estuary and the Garonne river, is gravel: stony soils that drain quickly after heavy rain and soak up heat during the day, keeping the vineyard warm into the evening. That extra warmth helps Cabernet ripen. Cabernet-dominated blends come from the Haut-Médoc, which includes famous villages like Margaux and Pauillac, and from Graves, which includes Pessac-Léognan. The best of these wines can age for a very long time.

Bordeaux's weather changes a lot from year to year. In some years Cabernet struggles to ripen even on the gravel, and that is where blending earns its keep: in a difficult year, the share of Merlot in the blend can go up. On Left Bank labels you may also see terms such as Château, Grand Cru Classé or Cru Bourgeois, which we cover in the lesson on label terms.

Still in France, the Languedoc-Roussillon is warm, and its weather is far more reliable than Bordeaux's, so Cabernet Sauvignon ripens every year. Here you will find both single-varietal Cabernet and blends with Merlot and other black grapes, usually labelled Pays d'Oc IGP.

Now California. The neighbouring regions of Napa Valley and Sonoma make many very good and outstanding Cabernets. Napa Valley has a warm, sunny climate and a long growing season, ideal for this grape. In the sub-regions of Oakville and Rutherford you find full-bodied wines with pronounced ripe black fruit and high, ripe tannins. Calistoga, in the far north of Napa Valley, is warmer still, and makes some of the ripest, fullest wines of all. The warmer inland parts of Sonoma can make similarly powerful wines. Even when labelled Cabernet Sauvignon, these wines may contain small amounts of other grapes.

At the other end of the scale, wines labelled simply California can be blended from grapes grown anywhere in the state, much of it from the hot, irrigated vineyards of the Central Valley. They are made to be drunk young, and any oak flavour usually comes from chips or staves.

In Chile, Cabernet Sauvignon is the most widely planted grape of all. Two key sub-regions sit within the broad Central Valley: the Maipo Valley and the Colchagua Valley. They stretch from the foothills of the Andes in the east to the coastal mountains in the west, with flatter, more fertile land on the valley floor, so producers have a huge choice of sites. More and more of them make very good to outstanding Cabernet Sauvignon, alone or blended with Merlot and Chile's speciality, Carmenère. Wines from the foothills often show distinctive mint and green pepper alongside black fruit and oak.

In South Africa, Stellenbosch is a high-quality, mountainous region where the climate goes from moderate to warm depending on altitude and sea breezes. So the styles range from fresh, herbal Cabernet to full-bodied wines with cooked fruit and high alcohol. Cabernet and Merlot are sometimes blended with the local grape Pinotage, to make what is known as a Cape Blend.

In Australia, Margaret River, in Western Australia, is warm but moderated by coastal breezes and plentiful winter rain. Its Cabernet, sometimes blended with Merlot, shows ripe black fruit and subtle oak. Coonawarra, a small region in South Australia, is cooled by cloud cover and southern breezes. Its Cabernet has a distinctive mint character, pronounced blackcurrant and smoke and cedar from oak, and can age for many years. Finally, in New Zealand's moderate Hawke's Bay, Cabernet needs the warmest sites to ripen, and is usually blended with the more widely grown Merlot, giving fresh red and black fruit with a hint of green pepper.

A memory tip for Cabernet Sauvignon: think of a blackcurrant bush with a sprig of mint, planted in a gravel bed. The blackcurrant is its fruit, the mint its herbal signature, and the gravel the warm, well-drained soil of the Left Bank that helps it ripen. Add a cedar box for the oak, and you have the classic picture.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Cabernet Sauvignon is a thick-skinned, late-ripening black grape for moderate and warm climates, giving deep-coloured wines with high acidity, high tannin, blackcurrant, black cherry and mint or green pepper; it is often oak-aged and can age for decades. Second, in Bordeaux it dominates the Left Bank blends of the Haut-Médoc, Margaux, Pauillac, Graves and Pessac-Léognan, thanks to warm, well-drained gravel, with Merlot added in difficult years. Third, key New World areas include Napa Valley with Oakville, Rutherford and Calistoga, Sonoma, Maipo and Colchagua in Chile, Stellenbosch, Margaret River, minty Coonawarra and Hawke's Bay.

In this lesson we meet Cabernet Sauvignon's great partner, and a star in its own right: Merlot. From its homeland in Bordeaux it has spread all over the world. It can make light, fruity reds to enjoy straight away, and also rich, concentrated wines that improve with oak and with years in bottle. We will see what the grape is like, how ripeness changes it, why it is such a good blending partner, and then we visit its key regions, from Saint-Émilion and Pomerol to California, Chile, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

First, the grape. Merlot is a black variety that grows in moderate and warm climates. A single-varietal Merlot is usually dry, with medium acidity and medium tannins: softer and rounder than Cabernet Sauvignon. Its character depends on ripeness. Just-ripe Merlot gives light to medium-bodied wines with fresh red fruit, strawberry and red plum, and a herbaceous touch of green bell pepper. Riper Merlot gives medium to full-bodied wines with cooked black fruit, blackberry and black plum. That riper style comes easily in a warm climate, but it can also be reached in a moderate climate by picking later.

In the winery, Merlot can make outstanding wines on its own, but it is also a famous blending grape. When it is blended with higher-tannin varieties such as Cabernet Sauvignon, it adds red fruit and lowers the overall tannin, so the wine is ready to drink sooner. Both oaked and unoaked styles exist. A light, fruity Merlot has little need for long barrel ageing. A fuller style can gain softness and complexity from oak. And the best Merlot-dominated wines age well, developing notes of dried fruit and tobacco.
