Now Bordeaux, Merlot's classic home, in south-west France. The climate is moderate, with plenty of rain from the nearby Atlantic, and Merlot is the region's most widely planted grape. Most wines are blends, mainly of Merlot and Cabernet Sauvignon. The proportions depend on the style the producer wants, but also on the soils and on each year's weather: in a year when Cabernet struggles, more Merlot goes into the blend.

Bordeaux is split by the Gironde estuary, where the Garonne and Dordogne rivers meet. West and south of the Gironde and Garonne lies the Left Bank, with the Médoc, Graves and Sauternes, where Cabernet Sauvignon usually leads. North and east of the Gironde and Dordogne lies the Right Bank, whose key districts are Saint-Émilion and Pomerol. Here Merlot is king. The outstanding wines of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol are full-bodied, with pronounced black fruit and oak, and they age well, developing dried fruit and tobacco.

A quick word on Bordeaux labels. The regional appellations, Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, can use grapes from anywhere in the region, and these wines are usually Merlot-led blends. Bordeaux Supérieur has slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing and minimum alcohol than plain Bordeaux. On the Right Bank, the appellation Saint-Émilion also contains a more prestigious level, Saint-Émilion Grand Cru.

Still in France, Merlot is planted widely in the warm Languedoc-Roussillon. You can find single-varietal Merlot at every quality level, as well as blends with Cabernet Sauvignon, Grenache and Syrah, usually labelled Pays d'Oc IGP.

Now California, a source of Merlot in every style and at every quality level. Blends are common, but single-varietal Merlot matters too. Styles range from fruity, medium-bodied wines simply labelled California to concentrated, full-bodied wines from the neighbouring regions of Napa Valley and Sonoma. Californian reds often show pronounced oak flavours, vanilla, coconut and smoke. The best are often aged in new barrels, while high-volume producers may use oak chips or staves.

In Chile, Merlot ripens easily in the warm, dry Central Valley, where high yields of fully ripe fruit are possible every year. This makes the Central Valley an important source of soft, medium-bodied Merlot for high-volume brands meant to be drunk young. But altitude can moderate the heat, so fresher styles are made there too.

In South Africa, Stellenbosch has built a strong reputation for complex, age-worthy reds from the classic Bordeaux grapes, Merlot among them. This mountainous region ranges from moderate to warm, depending on vineyard altitude and the influence of sea breezes. In Australia, Merlot has traditionally been a blending partner for Cabernet Sauvignon in high-quality wines, for example from Margaret River in Western Australia.

In New Zealand, most Merlot comes from Hawke's Bay, on the North Island. The climate is moderate with plentiful rain. Wines range from light and fruity to full-bodied and long-lived, and Merlot appears both on its own and blended with Cabernet Sauvignon. In fact, it is more widely grown there than Cabernet, which needs the warmest sites.

Merlot has sometimes been seen as a grape for high-volume brands, or only as a softener for Cabernet Sauvignon. Today producers around the world show that it can make impressive, complex, long-lived wines on its own. With its medium tannin and medium acidity, it is wonderfully versatile: fresh and unoaked at any price, or powerful and enriched by oak and bottle age.

A memory tip: if Cabernet Sauvignon is a firm handshake, Merlot is a warm hug. Softer tannins, medium acidity, plump plums and berries. And to place it on the map, remember that the Right Bank is the Merlot bank: Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, where the hug is at its richest.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Merlot is a black grape for moderate and warm climates, giving dry wines with medium acidity and medium tannin; just-ripe grapes give red fruit and green pepper, riper grapes give a fuller body and cooked black fruit. Second, it is Bordeaux's most planted grape and leads the Right Bank wines of Saint-Émilion and Pomerol, as well as most Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur, while it softens Cabernet Sauvignon in blends. Third, elsewhere it ranges from fruity, high-volume wines from Pays d'Oc, California and Chile's Central Valley to fuller, oaked wines from Napa Valley and Sonoma, and quality reds and blends from Stellenbosch, Margaret River and Hawke's Bay.

In this lesson we meet a grape with two passports. Syrah and Shiraz are exactly the same black variety: Syrah is its French name, and Shiraz is the name most used in Australia. We will look at what the grape is like, how climate shapes its two main styles, what happens in the winery, and then travel to its key regions: the Northern Rhône and the Languedoc in France, and the Barossa Valley and Hunter Valley in Australia.

First, the grape itself. Syrah has thick skins and small berries. Picture a bunch of little dark beads: lots of skin compared with juice. That is why its wines are deeply coloured and usually have medium to high tannins, along with medium to high acidity. To ripen fully it needs a moderate to warm climate. Its signature aromas are black fruit and, above all, black pepper. If you smell a red and think of a pepper mill, Syrah should be one of your first guesses.

Now, the two styles. In a moderate climate, Syrah is typically medium-bodied, with fresh black fruit such as black cherry and blackberry, some herbal notes and that peppery lift. This is the classic style of the Northern Rhône. In a warm climate, the same grape becomes full-bodied and high in alcohol, with cooked black fruit and liquorice. This riper style is common in the warmer parts of Australia. Same grape, two very different wines: the climate is the author.

Here is a handy clue for the shelf. Outside France and Australia, producers can choose either name, and the choice often hints at the style. A label saying Syrah usually promises the fresher, more peppery moderate-climate style. A label saying Shiraz usually signals a riper, richer, fuller wine. It is not a law, but it is a useful signal when you are choosing a bottle in a shop.

In the winery, Syrah makes many excellent single-varietal wines, but it is also a great team player. In blends it adds colour, black fruit and tannin. Its most common partner is Grenache, together with other grapes of the Southern Rhône, and these wines are sometimes called Rhône blends. Oak is often used for maturation: it softens the tannins and adds smoky and spicy notes. The best wines, with their intense flavours and firm tannins, can age in bottle for a decade or more, gaining dried fruit, leather, meat and earth.

Let's travel to France. The Northern Rhône is Syrah's classic home, and it is the only black grape permitted in the appellation wines of the area. The Rhône Valley follows the river south towards the Mediterranean, and in its northern part the valley is very narrow. The best vineyards climb steep slopes. The climate is only moderate, so the slope's aspect, facing the sun, helps the grapes ripen. Many slopes are so steep that no machine can work them: everything is done by hand, which makes these wines expensive to produce.

Three names matter here. Côte-Rôtie, in the far north, is the northern limit for ripening Syrah. Its very steep, stony slopes give complex, peppery wines that can develop for many years in bottle. Some producers keep an old tradition of fermenting a little Viognier, a white grape, together with the Syrah, which can add floral aromas. Further south is Hermitage, an appellation made of a single steep, south-facing hill. Around that hill lies Crozes-Hermitage: larger and flatter, with wines that are usually less intense and complex, but more affordable, because yields are higher and machines can be used.

Still in France, but further south and west, the Languedoc-Roussillon has a warm climate where Syrah ripens reliably. Here it is often blended with other grapes in appellation wines such as Minervois, or sold as a single variety under the Pays d'Oc regional label. Expect riper fruit and a fuller body than in the Northern Rhône.

Now to Australia, which has by far the largest plantings outside France. Shiraz is the most planted grape in the whole country. Much of it grows in warm inland regions and goes into inexpensive, high-volume wines labelled South Eastern Australia. At the top end, the warm Barossa Valley in South Australia is home to some of the oldest Shiraz vines in the world. Old vines give low yields of very concentrated fruit, and the wines are full-bodied, with high, ripe tannins, cooked blackberry and black cherry, black pepper and often vanilla and coconut from oak.

The Hunter Valley in New South Wales tells a different story. It lies quite far north, and in the southern hemisphere that means closer to the equator, so summers are very hot. But summer cloud cover and sea breezes slow down ripening. The result is a medium-bodied Shiraz with medium to high tannins and fresh black fruit, which develops earthy and meaty flavours with age. In Australia, Shiraz is mostly a single-varietal wine, but you will also find it blended with Cabernet Sauvignon or Grenache.

Why is this grape so popular? It can satisfy two kinds of drinker: those who love fresh, fragrant, peppery reds, and those who want full-bodied wines with cooked fruit. Its intense pepper also makes it a natural partner for strongly flavoured dishes. And styles keep growing: Australian producers even make sparkling red Shiraz, and many other countries are planting it and experimenting at every quality level.

A memory tip: think of a thermometer with two labels. At the cooler end, write Syrah, pepper, fresh black fruit, medium body, Northern Rhône and Hunter Valley. At the warmer end, write Shiraz, cooked black fruit, liquorice, full body, Barossa and the Languedoc. Most exam questions on this grape simply ask you where on that thermometer a wine sits.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Syrah and Shiraz are the same thick-skinned black grape, with black fruit, black pepper and medium to high tannins. Second, the Northern Rhône is its classic home, with Côte-Rôtie at the northern limit, Hermitage on a single south-facing hill and Crozes-Hermitage as the flatter, cheaper neighbour. Third, in Australia Barossa gives rich, full Shiraz from old vines, while the cloudy, breezy Hunter Valley gives a medium-bodied style that turns earthy and meaty with age.

In this lesson we learn to decode some of the most important words on European wine labels. These terms do not name a grape; they tell you where a wine comes from within a region, or how ripe its grapes were. We will start in Burgundy with Premier Cru and Grand Cru, move to Alsace and its Grand Cru appellations, then visit Bordeaux, with Bordeaux Supérieur, Cru Bourgeois and Grand Cru Classé, and finish in Germany, with its ripeness ladder and the words Trocken and Halbtrocken.

First, Burgundy. Here quality is built on place, and tiny differences between vineyards really matter. Think of a pyramid. At the base is the regional appellation, Bourgogne. Above it come the village wines, such as Meursault or Gevrey-Chambertin. Higher still are the Premier Cru vineyards, and at the very top the Grand Cru vineyards, the best individual sites of all. On the label, Premier Cru or Grand Cru tells you the wine comes from one of these recognised top vineyards.

Why are these vineyards better? Mostly because of slope and aspect. In the heart of Burgundy, the best red wine sites face south or south-east, catching extra sunlight and warmth. The grapes ripen more fully, and the wines are more concentrated and complex, able to age and develop notes like forest floor and mushroom. In cool Chablis, the Premier Cru and Grand Cru vineyards usually face south or south-west. And in villages such as Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet, these sites give outstanding Chardonnay that can develop hazelnut and mushroom over decades. Grand Cru wines are the most concentrated, the longest-lived and, because they are rare, the most expensive.

Now, Alsace, in north-eastern France. Most wines are sold under the regional Alsace appellation, but there are also Alsace Grand Cru appellations. These wines must come from specific vineyards, mostly on the steep foothills of the Vosges Mountains, facing east or south-east. They get more sunshine than vines on the flat plain, so the wines taste riper and are fuller-bodied. Typical grapes for these sites are Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer. Alsace wines are usually labelled with the grape variety, and since recent vintages the sweetness level must also be shown on a standard scale.

One more Alsace term is worth knowing: Vendanges Tardives, which means late harvest. It usually indicates a medium to sweet wine made from extra-ripe grapes, and it can appear on Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer, from either the regional or the Grand Cru appellations.

Let's head to Bordeaux, where labels combine an appellation with a few quality words. The broadest appellations are Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur. Both can use grapes from anywhere in the region, and they are usually blends led by Merlot. Bordeaux Supérieur simply follows slightly stricter rules on yields, ageing and minimum alcohol. So Supérieur here does not mean a famous site; it means a slightly more demanding version of the regional wine.

Next, the word Château. It does not have to mean a grand castle. It means an estate or producer, and it tells you the wine was made from grapes grown on the producer's own land, not bought in. Several parts of Bordeaux have drawn up classifications that rank the best wines from the best Châteaux. Classified wines may put Grand Cru Classé or Cru Classé on the label.

Some of those classifications have not been updated for a very long time, yet they are still seen as a strong sign of quality. Grand Cru Classé wines are among the most sought-after and expensive in Bordeaux, and they can usually mature in bottle for many years, even decades. And what about Médoc estates that were not classified? They can apply to use the term Cru Bourgeois. Most do not reach the prices of the classified Châteaux, but some are very good to outstanding, with long ageing potential.

A warning about a classic trap: Saint-Émilion Grand Cru is an appellation name on the Right Bank, a more prestigious part of Saint-Émilion. It is not the same thing as Grand Cru Classé. Always read the whole phrase on the label.

Finally, Germany. Its cool climate makes ripeness hard to achieve, so many label terms describe how ripe the grapes were at harvest, measured by their sugar. Landwein is the German regional, or protected geographical indication, category: usually light and dry to off-dry. Qualitätswein is a protected designation of origin wine from one of thirteen wine-growing areas, such as the Mosel or the Rheingau, with riper grapes and more flavour. Prädikatswein needs even riper grapes, all from a single wine-growing area, and comes in six categories.

Climb the ladder with me. Kabinett is the lightest and most delicate, with green apple, lime and blossom. Spätlese, meaning late harvest, is more concentrated and fuller, with riper citrus and some peach. Auslese, from selected extra-ripe bunches, shows apricot, mango and dried fruit. These three can be dry or have some sweetness; if dry, riper grapes mean more alcohol, so a dry Auslese is stronger than a dry Kabinett.

Then come the great sweet wines, whose sugars are concentrated on the vine and which stay low in alcohol. Beerenauslese uses bunches or berries concentrated by noble rot, with apricot, mango and honey. Eiswein comes from grapes frozen on the vine, with no noble rot at all, and needs the same minimum sugar as Beerenauslese. At the summit, Trockenbeerenauslese uses individual berries shrivelled by noble rot: rare and even more intense. Their high acidity lets them age for decades.

Two little words help when sweetness is unclear. Trocken means dry. Halbtrocken means the wine has some sweetness. A Beerenauslese is always sweet, so it needs no such word. A memory tip for the ladder: in German, Beeren means berries and Trocken means dry, so Trockenbeerenauslese is literally a selection of dried berries, the top of the ladder.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, in Burgundy and Alsace, Premier Cru and Grand Cru point to the best individual vineyards, usually on sunny slopes, with Grand Cru the very top. Second, in Bordeaux, Supérieur means slightly stricter regional rules, Grand Cru Classé and Cru Classé mean a classified estate, and Cru Bourgeois is for unclassified Médoc estates. Third, in Germany the Prädikat ladder runs from Kabinett to Trockenbeerenauslese, with Eiswein needing the same minimum sugar as Beerenauslese, while Trocken means dry and Halbtrocken means some sweetness.

In this lesson we meet three black grapes that are stars in their home regions. Gamay, almost entirely from Beaujolais. Grenache, called Garnacha in Spain, at home in the Southern Rhône, the south of France, Spain and Australia. And Tempranillo, Spain's most prized red grape. Along the way we will learn three label hierarchies, for Beaujolais, for the Rhône and for Spain, including the ageing terms Joven, Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva.

First, Gamay. It is a curious case: famous all over the world, yet its wines come almost entirely from one small region. Gamay gives high acidity, low to medium tannins and bright red fruit: raspberry, red cherry and red plum. It is usually made in inert vessels, such as stainless steel or concrete, so oak flavours are rare. Beaujolais lies just south of Burgundy, with a moderate climate. Winemakers there like techniques that draw out lots of colour but little tannin, and these methods can add aromas of banana and candy. The result is a light to medium-bodied, juicy red.

Beaujolais has a three-step pyramid. At the base, Beaujolais: grapes can come from anywhere in the region, but mostly from the flat, fertile south, where high yields give the lightest, simplest wines. Next, Beaujolais Villages, a group of villages in the north, where sloping vineyards catch more sun and warm, well-drained soils help ripening, so the wines have more flavour and body. At the top are the ten crus, areas inside the Villages zone with their own appellation; Fleurie is one of the best known. They are the most concentrated and structured. Most Beaujolais is for drinking young and is often served lightly chilled to make its fresh fruit sing, though some crus can develop in bottle.

Now, Grenache. It probably began in Spain as Garnacha, then spread across southern France and up the Rhône, where it became Grenache, the name most used elsewhere. It needs a warm climate. Ripe Grenache is high in sugar and low in acidity, so its wines are often high in alcohol. Its thin skins give low to medium tannins. Expect red fruit, strawberry, red plum and red cherry, sometimes with white pepper and liquorice. It shines when yields are kept under control.

Grenache has three habits worth remembering. Its red fruit makes it ideal for rosé by short maceration, from dry to medium, to drink chilled and young. It loves company: in France it is blended with Syrah, in Spain with Tempranillo, and these partners add the colour, acidity and tannin Grenache lacks. And in the cellar, simple versions are unoaked, while the best are matured in barrel, often old oak, so as not to cover its delicate fruit. With age it gains earth, meat and dried fruit.

Where do we find it? In the Southern Rhône the valley opens out and the warm climate lets Grenache ripen easily; reds are blends with several local grapes, Syrah included. The Rhône has a pyramid much like Beaujolais. Côtes du Rhône covers the whole valley but comes almost entirely from the south: simple, medium-bodied reds with red fruit and white pepper.

Côtes du Rhône Villages offers more concentration and complexity. At the top are the crus, in both north and south. The most famous southern cru is Châteauneuf-du-Pape, full-bodied and high in alcohol. Many of its vineyards are covered with large round stones that soak up heat by day and release it to the vines at night, helping Grenache ripen fully.

Further west, in Languedoc-Roussillon, Grenache gives red fruit and body to blends in Minervois, again with partners such as Syrah. To the east, Provence is famous for dry, pale rosé, mostly from Côtes de Provence, with Grenache as a key part of the blend.

In Spain, Garnacha adds body and fresh red fruit to the wines of Rioja and neighbouring Navarra, which is also known for dry rosé. The most powerful Garnacha comes from Priorat in Catalunya: a warm, dry area with very old vines giving tiny yields. These wines, usually blended, age for a long time, gaining dried fruit and caramel. And in Australia, the warm Barossa Valley and McLaren Vale have many very old Grenache vines that give concentrated red fruit and spice. Blends with Shiraz there can recall Châteauneuf-du-Pape in style and quality.

Now, Tempranillo, the backbone of many famous Spanish reds. Its wines are medium to full-bodied, with medium acidity and medium tannins, mixing red fruit, strawberry and red cherry, with black fruit, blackberry and black plum. It is versatile, from simple, fruity wines to complex wines built to age. For long ageing, a little of another grape is sometimes added to lift acidity and tannin. Tradition in much of Spain is maturation in small new oak barrels, bringing vanilla, smoke and cedar and softening the tannins. The best wines also rest in bottle before release and develop mushroom, leather and dried fruit.

Three Spanish regions matter. Rioja, in the north-east, has a moderate climate and is the most famous. It is usually a blend: Tempranillo dominates the best wines, Garnacha joins wines meant for early drinking, and other local grapes add tannin and acidity for long-lived wines. Ribera del Duero lies inland at high altitude: warm days and cool nights give very full-bodied Tempranillo with fresh black fruit, often very good to outstanding. Catalunya is a broad appellation making large volumes, from simple and fruity to powerful and oaked.

Finally, the Spanish ageing ladder. These terms apply to the whole country, not just Rioja. They set legal minimums, some regions are stricter, and many producers go further. Joven means young: no minimum ageing, usually released the year after harvest, all about primary fruit; in Rioja it is called Genérico. Crianza must spend time in oak, adding vanilla, smoke and coconut. Reserva ages longer in barrel and bottle: tannins soften, some fruit turns cooked or dried, and tertiary notes like mushroom appear. Gran Reserva has the longest minimums and the most pronounced oak and age character.

A word of caution: only grapes with enough fruit, acidity and tannin can survive long ageing. A modest wine aged too long tastes stale and short of fruit, which is why a producer may skip Gran Reserva in a weaker vintage. A memory tip: imagine a staircase from the cellar door. Joven is still on the doorstep, Crianza has entered the barrel room, Reserva has moved on to the bottle room, and Gran Reserva has stayed downstairs the longest.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Gamay is Beaujolais: high acidity, low tannin, red fruit, with a pyramid of Beaujolais, Beaujolais Villages and ten crus such as Fleurie. Second, Grenache is a warm-climate grape with high alcohol, low acidity and red fruit, central to Côtes du Rhône and Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Minervois, Provence rosé, Rioja, Navarra, Priorat and South Australia. Third, Tempranillo gives medium acidity and tannin with red and black fruit, shines in Rioja and Ribera del Duero, and Spain's ageing ladder runs Joven, Crianza, Reserva, Gran Reserva.

In this lesson we take a trip down Italy, from the Alps to the heel of the boot, meeting six black grapes. In the north, Nebbiolo and Barbera in Piemonte, and Corvina in the Veneto. In the centre, Sangiovese in Tuscany and Montepulciano in Abruzzo. In the south, Primitivo in Puglia. We will also learn how Italian wines are named, and what two label words mean: Classico and Riserva.

First, the setting. Northern Italy's vineyards sit in the foothills of the Alps and on flat river plains. The climate is generally moderate, and the best areas are sheltered by mountains to the north, with a wide variety of slopes and soils. Our first grape here is Nebbiolo. It is a grape with a firm backbone: high acidity and high tannins. Its aromas are distinctive: red cherry and red plum, dried herbs, and sometimes floral notes of rose and violet.

Those powerful tannins explain how Nebbiolo is made. It is often matured for a long time in oak to soften it. Some producers prefer old barrels, others choose new oak to add its own aromas. High acidity and tannin also give it a long life: the best wines improve in bottle and gain mushroom, tobacco and leather. Its most famous wine is Barolo, perhaps the best-known name in Piemonte, in the north-west. Only Nebbiolo is allowed. The area is a horseshoe-shaped valley with steep, south-facing vineyards, and the wines are full-bodied, pronounced in flavour, high in tannin and acidity, and built to age. Barbaresco, a smaller area to the north-east of Barolo, makes similarly powerful, long-lived Nebbiolo.

Barbera is Nebbiolo's friendlier neighbour in Piemonte. It shares the high acidity, but its tannins are only low to medium. Expect red cherry and red plum, sometimes with black pepper. Many Barbera wines are unoaked and fruity, while some producers mature them in oak for extra complexity. Many people consider Barbera d'Asti its finest wine. Because of its softer tannins, Barbera is enjoyable younger than Nebbiolo, and even the best usually have a shorter ageing potential.

Now east to the Veneto and Valpolicella, home of Corvina. Corvina gives high acidity, low to medium tannins and red cherry and plum. It usually dominates the blend, though other local grapes are allowed. A basic Valpolicella is light-bodied, fruity and simple, rarely sees new oak, and is for drinking young. Valpolicella Classico comes from the hillier heartland and has more body and complexity.

Then comes a special technique: appassimento. The grapes are picked and dried indoors, often in crates, which concentrates their sugars, acids, tannins and flavours. Amarone della Valpolicella is made from these partly dried grapes and is dry to off-dry: full-bodied, around fifteen percent alcohol, high in tannin, with fresh red cherry alongside dried fruit like prunes, raisins and figs. The best can age well in bottle. Recioto della Valpolicella also uses dried grapes, but here the sugar is so concentrated that yeast cannot ferment it all, so the wine is a sweet red. A related white, Recioto di Soave, uses the same drying method.

Let's move to central Italy. The Apennine Mountains run down the spine of the country like a dividing wall: to the west, Tuscany, where Sangiovese rules; to the east, Abruzzo, where Montepulciano is widely planted. The warm climate lets both make concentrated reds. Sangiovese gives dry wines with high tannins, high acidity, red cherry and red plum, and dried herbs. It grows all over Italy, but is most famous in Chianti, in central Tuscany, where it dominates, often with small amounts of other black grapes.

Chianti covers a wide area in the Apennine foothills and quality varies: many wines are simple, inexpensive and not for ageing. Chianti Classico lies higher up, giving Sangiovese a long ripening season. A typical Chianti Classico is medium-bodied with pronounced red fruit and dried herbs, often oak-matured to soften the tannins and add cloves and cedar; the best gain meat and leather in bottle. Further south, in the warm, sunny town of Montalcino, Brunello di Montalcino is powerful and full-bodied, with very high tannin and acidity. It must spend a long time in oak before release and can age for a very long time. Brunello is simply the local name for Sangiovese.

Across the mountains, Montepulciano gives deeply coloured wines with medium acidity, high tannins and black fruit: black plum and black cherry. Note the contrast with Sangiovese: black fruit instead of red, medium acidity instead of high. It is best known as Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, from east-central Italy. Abruzzo makes large volumes of inexpensive, simple, fruity wine for early drinking; more concentrated versions may spend a short time in oak. And a classic trap: Montepulciano is also the name of a Tuscan town, but the grape we mean here is the one from Abruzzo.

Finally, the south. Primitivo is the same grape that California calls Zinfandel. It needs warmth, and as it ripens its flavours move from red to black fruit; some berries may even start to shrivel on the vine before others are ripe, adding sugar and dried-fruit notes. Warm Puglia is an important source of soft, fruity, dry red for high-volume brands. But with controlled yields, Puglia also makes very good to outstanding Primitivo, often excellent value for money.

Now the labels. Some Italian wines are named after a place only: Barolo, Barbaresco, Valpolicella, Chianti. Others join grape and place: Barbera d'Asti means Barbera from Asti, and Montepulciano d'Abruzzo means Montepulciano from Abruzzo. So you must learn which grape hides behind each place name. Then two useful words. Classico is about place: the grapes come from the historic heart of an area, often its hilliest part, giving more concentrated wines. Riserva is about time: a quality wine aged for a minimum number of months before release. A Chianti Classico Riserva can carry both, and may already show some tertiary notes when sold.

A memory tip: think of Italy's reds as a family photo. Nebbiolo is the stern grandparent, with a grip that lasts for decades. Barbera is the cheerful cousin, all freshness and soft hugs. Corvina is the one who dries fruit in the attic. Sangiovese is the herb-scented Tuscan, Montepulciano the dark, sturdy one across the hills, and Primitivo the sun-loving relative who moved to California and changed name.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, in Piemonte Nebbiolo makes Barolo and Barbaresco, with high acidity and high tannin, while Barbera, best in Barbera d'Asti, has high acidity but soft tannins. Second, in the Veneto Corvina makes light Valpolicella and, from dried grapes, dry Amarone and sweet Recioto. Third, Sangiovese, with high acidity, tannin, red fruit and herbs, makes Chianti, Chianti Classico and Brunello di Montalcino; Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is dark and black-fruited; Primitivo rules in Puglia; and remember: Classico is place, Riserva is time.

In this lesson we cross to the Americas and South Africa to meet four black grapes that have become national signatures. Zinfandel in California, Carmenère in Chile, Malbec in Argentina and Pinotage in South Africa. These countries also succeed with famous international grapes, but their specialities give them something nobody else has, a point of difference on a very crowded wine shelf. We will finish with a label term from South Africa: the Cape Blend.

First, Zinfandel. It is the same grape that Italy, especially Puglia, calls Primitivo. It is a black grape that needs a warm climate. As it ripens, its flavours move from red fruit, strawberry and raspberry, to black fruit, black plum, blackberry and blueberry. It also ripens unevenly: some berries in a bunch can start to shrivel like raisins before the others are ripe. That brings high sugar levels and dried-fruit flavours, prune and raisin.

In California, Zinfandel makes two very different wines. The first is White Zinfandel, which, despite its name, is pink: a medium-sweet rosé. It is usually made by short maceration, a brief contact between juice and skins. To keep some sweetness, the yeasts are removed before fermentation has finished, so the wine stays low in alcohol, typically eight to ten percent. It smells simply of strawberry and raspberry.

The second is red Zinfandel, made the standard red way: fermentation runs to completion with the juice in contact with the skins throughout. It is often matured in oak to soften the tannins and add complexity. A typical red Zinfandel is dry, full-bodied and high in alcohol, with medium to high acidity and tannin, and pronounced aromas of raspberry, blueberry and blackberry, raisin and prune, plus vanilla and coffee from oak. California also has some very old Zinfandel vines that give small crops of highly concentrated fruit, and those wines can develop earth and meat in bottle. Here is a quick label clue: a Zinfandel with low alcohol is almost certainly the rosé; a high figure means the red.

Now, Chile and Carmenère. Carmenère was born in Bordeaux, but it is now rarely found there, and it is widely grown in Chile. It needs a long, sunny growing season, and even in Chile it struggles to ripen except in the warmest, sunniest sites of the Central Valley. Picked too early, it gives pungent green aromas, green bell pepper and tomato leaf. Fully ripe, it shows fresh blackberry.

A typical Carmenère is deeply coloured, with medium to high acidity, high tannins and full body. It is often matured in oak barrels, which soften the tannins and add coffee and chocolate. The best examples develop leather and earth with age. You can find it on its own, but it is more often blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.

Next, Argentina and Malbec, the country's most important black grape. Like Carmenère, it comes from France, from the south-west, and it has adapted beautifully to the warmer South American climate. It grows across Argentina, but most of it is in Mendoza, a high-altitude region. Malbec usually gives deeply coloured, full-bodied wines with high tannins and black fruit, blackberry and black plum. New oak adds softness and spice, clove and vanilla, and the best wines gain dried fruit and meat in bottle. It is often a single-varietal wine, but blends with Cabernet Sauvignon or Merlot are common too.

Now South Africa and Pinotage. Unlike the two French grapes we just met, Pinotage was created specially for South Africa's warm, dry climate. It is closely related to Pinot Noir and shares its red fruit: strawberry, raspberry and red cherry. It is grown throughout the Western Cape. Its wines usually have medium tannins and high acidity.

Pinotage comes in a wide range of styles. At one end, fruity, medium-bodied reds with strawberry and red cherry. At the other, powerful, full-bodied wines with concentrated red plum and blackberry. When it is made in contact with oak, it can take on pronounced aromas of coffee, chocolate and smoke. It is bottled on its own or blended with grapes such as Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, and these blends that include Pinotage are commonly called Cape Blends. You may see that term on the label next to Western Cape.

How can you recognise these wines in a shop? Labels usually show the grape, the region and the country. Look for Mendoza and Malbec together, for Carmenère with the words wine of Chile, and for Pinotage or Cape Blend with Western Cape and wine of South Africa. For Zinfandel, check the colour words and the alcohol figure to tell the rosé from the red.

A memory tip: match each grape to a dessert-and-coffee image. Carmenère and Pinotage both like coffee and chocolate from oak, while Malbec prefers clove and vanilla spice. Then add one green warning: only Carmenère gives green bell pepper when it is picked too early. And Zinfandel is the one that brings raisins to the table.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Zinfandel, the same grape as Primitivo, ripens unevenly, giving dried fruit; in California it makes medium-sweet, low-alcohol White Zinfandel rosé and full-bodied, high-alcohol dry reds, with old vines giving the most concentrated wines. Second, Carmenère from Chile's Central Valley needs a long sunny season, shows green pepper if underripe and blackberry when ripe, while Malbec, mostly from high-altitude Mendoza, is deep, full and tannic with black fruit. Third, Pinotage was bred for South Africa, is related to Pinot Noir, has high acidity and medium tannins, and blends that include it are called Cape Blends.

In this lesson we meet ten white grapes that are each tied to particular places. To keep them tidy, we will sort them into three families. First, the versatile ones that make both dry and sweet wines: Chenin Blanc, Sémillon and Furmint. Second, the aromatic ones: Gewurztraminer, Viognier and Albariño. Third, four Italian locals: Cortese, Garganega, Verdicchio and Fiano. Along the way we will meet the label words Classico and Aszú.

Let's start with Chenin Blanc, one of the most versatile white grapes in the world. It grows in cool, moderate and warm climates, and its flavours follow ripeness: green apple and lemon when just ripe, then peach, then pineapple and mango. It has naturally high acidity, which suits late harvesting, and it is prone to noble rot. So Chenin can be dry, off-dry, medium or sweet, oaked or unoaked, and the best can age for many years thanks to that acidity.

Its classic French home is Vouvray, in the Loire Valley, where Chenin is the only grape allowed. Vouvray comes in every style: dry, off-dry, medium, sweet and even sparkling. Dry versions often taste of fresh apple. Off-dry and medium wines are labelled Demi-Sec. Sweeter ones come from extra-ripe or noble-rotted grapes and show stone and tropical fruit. Whatever the style, Vouvray is usually unoaked to keep the fruit fresh, and the best gain honey and dried fruit with age.

In South Africa, Chenin is the most planted white grape, prized for keeping its acidity in a warm climate. Inexpensive Western Cape blends are dry, medium-bodied, with peach, pineapple and sometimes vanilla from oak chips or staves. Old vines give concentrated, outstanding wines with pineapple, mango, smoke and vanilla, and some producers blend it with Viognier for a floral touch.

Next, Sémillon, spelt with an accent in France and without one in English-speaking countries. It likes moderate and warm climates. Young, it is simple: apple, lemon and grass. Depending on ripeness, it can be light or full-bodied, with medium to high acidity, and it can age into dried fruit, nuts and honey. In Bordeaux it is often blended with Sauvignon Blanc, for dry and sweet wines, adding body and ageing potential.

Its most famous sweet wine is Sauternes, a small area of Bordeaux. Sémillon is very prone to noble rot, so it is the key grape there. A typical Sauternes is sweet, full-bodied, medium to high in alcohol, with high acidity to balance, and pronounced apricot plus smoke and vanilla from oak. It can age for many years, gaining dried fruit, honey and caramel.

In Australia, the Hunter Valley makes a unique dry Semillon: grapes are picked early in this warm region, while sugar is low and acidity high, then fermented in inert vessels and bottled young. Light-bodied and low in alcohol, it tastes quite neutral at first, but after several years it develops honey and nuts. The Barossa Valley makes Semillon in several styles, from Hunter-like wines to full-bodied, oaked ones.

The last of our versatile trio is Furmint, grown mostly in Hungary. High acidity and great susceptibility to noble rot make it ideal for sweet wine. It is the most planted grape of Tokaj, in north-east Hungary. Tokaj makes dry and medium wines too, but it is famous for Tokaji Aszú, a sweet wine from noble-rotted grapes, with Furmint as the main grape, often joined by other local varieties. Aszú is always sweet, and the number of puttonyos on the label hints at how sweet: most are five or six puttonyos, and six is sweeter. Long oak ageing gives an amber colour, with apricot, citrus, vanilla, smoke, caramel and nuts, high acidity, a full body and a long finish.

Now the aromatic family. Gewurztraminer grows best in cool to moderate climates and makes powerfully scented wines, from dry to sweet. It builds up a lot of sugar, so dry versions are high in alcohol. Expect full body, low to medium acidity, and pronounced rose, peach, apricot and above all lychee. It is usually unoaked to protect those aromas, and the best gain honey and dried fruit with age. Its most famous home is Alsace, where it makes some of the region's top Grand Cru wines alongside Riesling and Pinot Gris.

Viognier is aromatic too, mostly from moderate climates. It is typically dry, with low to medium acidity, high alcohol and medium to full body, with blossom, peach and apricot. Most is made in inert vessels, but unusually for an aromatic grape, some is oak-aged. Some of the finest come from Condrieu, in the Northern Rhône, an appellation devoted to single-varietal Viognier, where a light touch of vanilla from oak is common, never allowed to hide the floral perfume. Viognier is fashionable both alone and as a blending partner, adding body and floral notes.

Albariño is the fresh one. It grows in Rías Baixas, in the north-west corner of Spain, near the Atlantic. The climate is moderate, and cooler, wetter and cloudier than most of Spain, perfect for refreshing whites. A typical Albariño is dry, with high acidity, medium body, lemon and grapefruit plus peach and apricot. It is usually unoaked and drunk young, sometimes with a little lees contact for extra body and complexity. Its popularity is growing, and it is now planted in suitable sites outside Spain.

Finally, four Italian whites. Cortese makes Gavi, in Piemonte: dry, light-bodied, high acidity, with blossom, apple, pear and lemon, made in inert vessels, unoaked and ready on release. Garganega, in the Veneto, is the key grape of Soave and Soave Classico: dry, medium-bodied, high acidity, apple, pear, lemon and peach, also unoaked. Most Soave is for drinking young, but the best Soave Classico can gain honey and almond. Here, Classico means the historic heartland of the area. And Recioto di Soave is a sweet white made from grapes dried by appassimento.

Verdicchio comes from the Marche, on Italy's east coast; its most famous wine is Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi. It is dry, high in acidity, medium-bodied, with apple, pear, lemon and a herbal note of fennel. Most are simple and for drinking young, but outstanding ones can develop honey and nuts. Fiano, from southern Italy, is best known in Fiano di Avellino, from mountainous Campania. It has medium acidity, medium to full body, peach, melon and mango. Many are made in inert vessels, but some show bread and biscuit from lees or smoke from oak, and the best can develop honey.

A memory tip: picture three tables. On the first, a dessert table with Chenin, Sémillon and Furmint, the grapes that love noble rot and keep their acidity. On the second, a flower stall: lychee and rose for Gewurztraminer, blossom and apricot for Viognier, a sea breeze and grapefruit for Albariño. On the third, an Italian aperitivo: crisp Gavi, almond-tinged Soave, fennel-scented Verdicchio and rounder, tropical Fiano.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Chenin Blanc, from Vouvray and South Africa, Sémillon, from Sauternes and the Hunter Valley, and Furmint, from Tokaj, all have high acidity or noble rot potential and can make dry or great sweet wines; Aszú is always sweet, measured in puttonyos. Second, Gewurztraminer from Alsace and Viognier from Condrieu are full, floral and fairly low in acidity, while Albariño from Rías Baixas is crisp and fresh. Third, Italy's whites: Cortese for Gavi, Garganega for Soave and sweet Recioto di Soave, Verdicchio for the Castelli di Jesi, and Fiano for Avellino.

In this lesson we find out where the bubbles come from. Bubbles are simply carbon dioxide dissolved in the wine. A producer could pump the gas in, but most quality producers capture the carbon dioxide that fermentation makes naturally. We will follow the base wine, the second fermentation, the traditional method in the bottle and the tank method, and then meet the key wines: Champagne, Cava, Prosecco and Asti, plus sparkling wines from South Africa, the USA, Australia and New Zealand. And we will decode Brut, Demi-Sec, vintage and non-vintage.

Almost every sparkling wine starts life as a still base wine. It is usually dry, high in acidity and low in alcohol, and it is generally a blend: of different grapes, different vineyards, sometimes different vintages. To create the bubbles, the producer adds sugar and yeast to this dry wine, starting a second fermentation. The yeast turns the sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, raising the alcohol by about one and a half percent. The trick is to do it in a sealed vessel, so the gas cannot escape and has to dissolve in the wine. That vessel is either a bottle or a tank.

First, bottle fermentation, and its most respected form, the traditional method, used most famously for Champagne and Cava, and anywhere a label says Traditional Method or Méthode Traditionnelle. The base wine, sugar and yeast go into a strong bottle sealed with a crown cap, like a beer bottle. The bottle lies on its side while the second fermentation happens inside. When it ends, the dead yeast forms a sediment called lees.

Now the magic. Over months and years, the lees slowly break down. This is called yeast autolysis, and it gives the wine aromas of bread and biscuit. The longer the wine rests on its lees, the more intense these autolytic aromas become. Think of a bakery slowly filling the bottle.

But nobody wants a cloudy glass, so the lees must come out. First comes riddling: the bottle is turned very slowly from horizontal to upside down, so the sediment slides into the neck. This was once done by hand; today it is mostly done by a machine called a gyropalette, a cube that moves hundreds of bottles at once. Then disgorgement: the neck is frozen, trapping the lees in a plug of ice. When the crown cap is removed, the pressure pushes the ice plug out.

Before resealing, the bottle is topped up with a mixture of wine and usually sugar, called the liqueur d'expédition. Adding it is called dosage, a word that also means the amount of sugar added, and it decides the final sweetness. Most traditional-method wines are Brut: a tiny amount of sugar is added, but the wine tastes dry thanks to its high acidity and lively bubbles. Demi-Sec means medium sweet, with more sugar in the mix. Finally the bottle gets a thick cork and a wire cage.

Let's meet the wines. Champagne, from northern France, is usually a blend of Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier. The cool climate is ideal for a base wine with low alcohol and high acidity. Most Champagne blends wines from several vintages for consistency, and is called non-vintage. The least expensive spend the legal minimum of twelve months on lees: dry, high in acidity, with apple and light autolytic notes.

Better ones, from riper grapes and longer lees ageing, show apple, lemon, toast and biscuit. In exceptional years, the best grapes may make a Vintage Champagne, aged long on its lees and then in bottle, adding nuts and honey. These are rare and very expensive. One curiosity: Champagne and Cava are among the few European wines that need not show their protected designation of origin on the label.

Cava is Spain's traditional-method sparkling wine, made in certain regions, but mostly in Catalunya. It uses mainly local Spanish grapes, though Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are allowed and add fruit and acidity. The warm climate means grapes may be picked early to keep acidity. The base wine tastes lightly of apple and lemon, and most Cava spends less time on lees than Champagne, so its autolytic notes are subtle. A few large brands make lots of simple non-vintage Cava, but many smaller producers make very good wines with long lees ageing.

South Africa, the USA, Australia and New Zealand also make fine bottle-fermented wines, usually from their coolest regions, often with Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. The best are intense and complex with a long finish, and their extra sunshine gives slightly riper fruit than Champagne. In South Africa, the term Cap Classique means traditional method, sometimes from Champagne grapes, sometimes from others such as Chenin Blanc.

Now the tank method, used when the winemaker does not want autolytic flavours, for example with aromatic grapes. The base wine goes into a sealed tank with yeast and sugar, the second fermentation happens there, the lees are filtered out, and the wine is bottled under pressure with a thick cork and wire cage. It still tastes mainly of the base wine, and it is much cheaper and less labour-intensive. Prosecco, from north-east Italy, is usually made this way from the Glera grape: light to medium-bodied, with pear, melon and blossom, typically dry or off-dry. There is also a rosé version, mostly Glera with a little Pinot Noir for colour.

For sweet sparkling wines there is a variation, often called the Asti method. It does not start with a dry base wine. Grape juice ferments in a pressurised tank; at first the gas escapes, then partway through the tank is sealed to keep the bubbles. The yeast is filtered out before all the sugar is used, so the wine is sweet, low in alcohol and sparkling. Asti, from Piemonte, is made this way from Moscato: light-bodied, with blossom, grape, peach and pear, and usually fully sparkling. Sweet, low-alcohol Moscato sparklers made like this are popular worldwide.

A memory tip: bottle method means bakery, tank method means fruit bowl. If a sparkling wine smells of toast and biscuit, it probably spent time on its lees in the bottle. If it smells purely of fresh fruit and flowers, like pear, melon or grapes, it most likely comes from a tank. And if it is sweet and very low in alcohol, think of the Asti method.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, the bubbles come from a second fermentation in a sealed vessel, and in the traditional method the lees give bread and biscuit through autolysis, followed by riddling, disgorgement and a dosage that makes the wine Brut or Demi-Sec. Second, Champagne, from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Meunier, Cava from Catalunya and Cap Classique are all traditional method; most are non-vintage, while vintage wines come from a single exceptional year. Third, the tank method keeps fresh fruit, as in Prosecco from Glera, and the Asti method gives sweet, low-alcohol Asti from Moscato.

In this lesson we travel to southern Spain to discover Sherry. First, what a fortified wine is. Then how Sherry is made, from a simple dry base wine to the solera. Then the two great ways of ageing: under a layer of yeast called flor, or in contact with oxygen. Finally we will sort out the styles: Fino, Amontillado and Oloroso, and the sweet ones, Pale Cream, Medium, Cream and Pedro Ximénez.

A fortified wine is a wine with extra alcohol added. Historically, fortification made wine stronger so it would not spoil on long journeys. Sherry and Port are the two classic examples, but they use fortification differently. Port is fortified during fermentation, which keeps it sweet. Sherry is fortified after fermentation has finished, so the base wine is fully dry. Most Sherry is therefore dry, and the sweet styles are usually sweetened later.

Sherry comes from the area around the town of Jerez de la Frontera in southern Spain. Almost every style starts from the same humble point: a simple, dry white base wine made from Palomino, a local white grape. Once fermentation is complete, grape alcohol is added, and the wine enters the solera.

What is a solera? It is a system of old oak casks holding wines of different ages. As the wines age, they are continually blended together: some wine is drawn from the oldest casks for bottling, and those casks are topped up with younger wine, which in turn is topped up with even younger wine. Picture a family where the elders constantly teach the younger ones. The result is a consistent, complex, mature style year after year. And it is in the solera that each Sherry develops its own personality.

The three key dry styles are Fino, Oloroso and Amontillado. They differ mostly because of how, and how long, they age in the solera. Let's begin with Fino. The base wine is fortified to about fifteen percent alcohol, then put into the solera, where a thick white layer of yeast called flor grows on the surface. The flor acts like a blanket, protecting the wine from oxygen. This is called biological ageing.

A Fino is pale lemon in colour, with aromas of apple and almond and pronounced bread dough notes from the flor. It is fresh and delicate, so once bottled it loses its freshness quickly: drink it as soon as possible, and serve it chilled.

Oloroso takes the opposite road. The base wine is fortified to about seventeen percent alcohol, a strength at which flor cannot survive. Without that protective blanket, the wine ages oxidatively, in contact with oxygen. Over the years it turns brown and develops dried fruit, raisin and prune, along with notes of deliberate oxidation, walnut and caramel.

Amontillado sits in between. It begins life like a Fino, ageing under flor for a time. Then it is fortified again to about seventeen percent, which kills the flor, and from then on it ages oxidatively until bottling. So an Amontillado is clearly deeper in colour than a Fino and combines both worlds: bread dough from the flor, and walnut and caramel from oxygen.

Now the sweet styles. Dry Sherries can be sweetened, but then the label must use a different or additional term. Pale Cream is a sweetened Fino. Medium and Cream are names often used for sweetened Amontillado or Oloroso. And then there is PX, short for Pedro Ximénez. It is made from white Pedro Ximénez grapes dried in the sun to concentrate their sugar, then fortified and aged oxidatively in the solera. The result is deep brown and very sweet, with pronounced fig, prune and raisin, liquorice and molasses. PX is often used to sweeten Cream Sherries.

A memory tip: think of flor as a duvet. Fino sleeps under the duvet all its life, so it stays pale and fresh. Oloroso never gets a duvet, so oxygen browns it into walnuts and caramel. Amontillado sleeps under the duvet for a while, then someone pulls it off. And the alcohol is the switch: about fifteen percent lets flor live, about seventeen percent kills it.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Sherry comes from around Jerez, starts as a dry Palomino base wine, is fortified after fermentation and ages in a solera of old oak casks. Second, Fino ages under flor at about fifteen percent and is pale, fresh, almondy and bready, to drink chilled and soon; Oloroso, at about seventeen percent, ages oxidatively and turns brown with dried fruit, walnut and caramel; Amontillado does both. Third, sweet styles are Pale Cream from Fino, Medium and Cream from Amontillado or Oloroso, and PX from sun-dried Pedro Ximénez grapes.

In this lesson we sail up the Douro River in Portugal to discover Port. We will see how every Port is made, why it is always sweet, and how ageing creates its two families of styles: the deep, fruity ruby styles and the brown, nutty tawny styles. Along the way we will meet Ruby, Reserve Ruby, Late Bottled Vintage, Vintage and Tawny, and learn how to tell them apart.

Port is a sweet fortified wine from grapes grown in the Upper Douro region of Portugal. It is made from a blend of local black grape varieties, and most Ports also blend wines from several vintages. Remember the key difference from Sherry: Sherry is fortified after fermentation, so it starts dry. Port is fortified during fermentation, so it always stays sweet.

All Port follows the same basic recipe. Right after harvest, the first task is to pull out colour and tannin from the grape skins quickly, because the fermentation will be short. Traditionally this was done by people treading the grapes with their feet in shallow tanks; today machines can do the same job. Then, partway through fermentation, grape spirit is added. The alcohol kills the yeast, the fermentation stops, and the wine is left sweet, with natural grape sugar, and high in alcohol.

Next the wine is matured before blending and bottling, and just as with Sherry, maturation decides the style. Think of two roads. On the first road, the wine is protected and keeps its deep colour and fruit: these are the ruby styles. On the second, the wine meets oxygen slowly over many years and turns brown and nutty: these are the tawny styles.

Let's take the ruby road first. Ruby-style Ports are deeply coloured and fruity. After fortification they age for a while in large vessels, traditionally big old oak casks, sometimes stainless steel tanks, and are bottled ready to drink. Their typical flavours are cooked black fruits: black cherry and blackberry.

The simplest is Ruby Port: inexpensive, sweet, simple and fruity, with lower tannins than other ruby styles and often some red fruit alongside the black. One step up is Reserve Ruby, made from better wines with more flavour intensity, and sometimes matured longer to soften and blend in the added alcohol. Late Bottled Vintage, or LBV, is similar in style to a Reserve Ruby, but all its wine comes from a single year.

At the top of the ruby road is Vintage Port, made from the very best wines of a single exceptional year. It is high in tannins and very concentrated, and it is built to age in bottle for at least twenty years, often much longer. With time, its colour moves from ruby to garnet, and it develops dried fruit, leather and forest floor. Because it ages in the bottle, it throws a thick sediment and needs decanting before serving. Vintage Port is not made every year: producers only declare a vintage in the best years.

Now the tawny road. Tawny Ports take their name from their tawny, brownish colour. The best get that colour from long oxidative ageing in small barrels. Year after year, the wine grows browner and develops dried fruit plus notes of deliberate oxidation: walnut, coffee and caramel. These wines often carry an age indication of ten, twenty, thirty or forty years, and some are even older. But be careful: an inexpensive wine labelled simply Tawny Port is a different thing: simple, fruity, low in tannin and pale in colour.

A memory tip: imagine two cellars. In the ruby cellar, the wine waits in large containers or in the bottle, keeping its dark colour and black fruit, and the best of it, Vintage Port, keeps evolving in the bottle and needs decanting. In the tawny cellar, the wine lives in small barrels breathing oxygen, so it fades towards brown and tastes of walnuts, coffee and caramel. Small barrel, more air, more brown.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, Port comes from the Upper Douro in Portugal, is made from local black grapes, and is fortified with grape spirit during fermentation, which leaves it sweet and high in alcohol. Second, the ruby styles are deep and fruity with cooked black fruit: Ruby is simple, Reserve Ruby is more intense, LBV comes from a single year, and Vintage Port, from a declared exceptional year, ages for decades in bottle and needs decanting. Third, Tawny Port ages oxidatively in small barrels, turning brown with walnut, coffee and caramel, often with an age statement of ten to forty years, while basic Tawny is simple and pale.

In this lesson we look after wine before it reaches the glass. A wine can be beautifully made and still disappoint if it has been kept badly. We will cover the three golden rules of storage, temperature, light and the position of the bottle, and then see how to keep an opened bottle fresh, using the fridge, vacuum systems and inert gas.

First, why does storage matter so much? Wine is alive in a quiet way: it keeps reacting to its surroundings. Stored badly, it first loses some of its character, especially its freshness and its fruit. Then, if the problem continues, it can develop real faults. Every tradition of storing and serving wine, however old or local, should aim at one simple goal: getting the wine to the table in the best possible condition.

Rule number one is temperature. For long-term storage, wine wants to be cool, and above all it wants a constant temperature. Extreme cold and extreme heat can both harm it, and so can big swings up and down. Think of the kitchen: the oven goes on, the heating goes off, the sun comes through the window. A bottle on top of the fridge lives through a little heatwave every day. A cellar, a cool cupboard or a wine cabinet is a much calmer home.

What happens if a wine gets too warm? We call it heat damage. The wine quickly loses its freshness, and the fruit you expect simply is not there; it can taste flat, dull or cooked. The same thing can happen whether the bottle waits for months in a warm room or a single afternoon in a hot car, so think about short-term storage too.

Rule number two is light. Keep wine away from strong sunshine and from bright artificial light. Both the light itself and the heat it gives off can rob a wine of its fruit character. A bottle displayed in a shop window under spotlights, or standing on a sunny windowsill at home, may look lovely, but it may reach the glass tired and lifeless.

Rule number three is the position of the bottle, and it depends on the closure. A bottle sealed with a cork should lie on its side. That way the wine stays in contact with the cork and keeps it moist. If the cork dries out, it can shrink and let air into the bottle; the wine then oxidises and loses its fruit. A bottle with a screwcap has no such problem, so it can be stored standing up.

Now, what about a bottle you have already opened? From the moment the cork comes out, the wine starts to react with the air. Slowly it becomes stale: less lively, less fresh, less fruity. The simplest remedy is free: put the cork back in and keep the bottle in the fridge. The cold slows those reactions down, so the wine stays fresher for longer, and this works for reds as well as whites, as long as you let the red warm up a little before drinking.

If you want a partly full bottle to last even longer, there are two simple systems. Vacuum systems use a small hand pump and a special stopper to remove air from the bottle. Inert gas systems fill the space above the wine with a gas such as nitrogen or argon. These gases are called inert because they do not react with the wine; they form a protective layer so that the wine does not touch the air. Both systems aim at the same goal: less contact with air, more freshness.

A memory tip: picture a wine's ideal home as a quiet, dark, cool bedroom where the bottle lies down to sleep. Cool and steady, like a cellar. Dark, with the curtains drawn. And lying down, if it wears a cork. Once it has been woken up and opened, give it a blanket against the air, with the fridge, a vacuum pump or a layer of inert gas.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, store wine at a cool, constant temperature, avoiding extreme heat, extreme cold and big swings; too much heat causes heat damage, with lost freshness and fruit. Second, keep it away from strong sunshine and bright artificial light, and lay cork-sealed bottles on their side so the cork stays moist, while screwcaps can stand up. Third, an opened bottle goes stale as it reacts with air: re-cork it and refrigerate it, or use a vacuum pump or an inert gas such as nitrogen or argon to keep the air away.

In this lesson we become the host. We will set the right service temperature for each style, open a still and a sparkling wine safely, decant a wine with a deposit, choose and prepare the glasses, check the wine before pouring, and finally learn to spot three common faults: cork taint, a failed closure and heat damage.

Let's start with temperature. As a general rule, white, rosé and sparkling wines are served chilled, and reds are served lightly chilled or at room temperature. But room temperature is a slippery idea: with central heating and air conditioning it can vary a lot, so it is better to think in ranges of degrees. And remember that these are guidelines, not laws. If a guest prefers a wine warmer or cooler, a good host respects that.

Here are the ranges, in degrees Celsius, from coldest to warmest. Sweet wines, such as Sauternes, are served well chilled, six to eight degrees. Sparkling wines, such as Champagne, are also well chilled, six to ten. Light and medium-bodied whites and rosés, such as Pinot Grigio, are chilled, seven to ten. Full-bodied whites, such as an oaked Chardonnay, are lightly chilled, ten to thirteen, because too much cold would hide their richness. Light-bodied reds, such as Beaujolais, sit at thirteen to eighteen, lightly chilled or at room temperature. Medium and full-bodied reds, such as Shiraz, are at room temperature, fifteen to eighteen.

Two practical tips. To keep a wine cold until the last glass, use an insulated container or an ice bucket, and fill the bucket with ice and cold water, not ice alone, because water surrounds the bottle and chills it far better. And if a red is too cold, never warm it next to a radiator; heat damages its flavours. Simply bring it into the room where it will be served and let it warm up naturally.

Now, opening a still wine with a cork, natural or synthetic. Remove the top of the capsule with a foil cutter or the little knife on a waiter's friend corkscrew, then wipe the neck with a cloth. Put the screw into the centre of the cork, turn it in, and draw the cork out gently. Finally, wipe the inside and outside of the neck again before pouring.

Sparkling wine needs more care, because the bottle holds a lot of pressure. Chilling reduces it, but even a cold cork can fly out and hurt someone. So from the moment you loosen the wire cage, keep your hand over the cork. Remove the foil, loosen the cage, then hold the bottle at an angle, the cork in one hand and the base in the other. Here is the trick: turn the bottle, not the cork. Hold the cork firmly so the pressure cannot push it out too fast. The goal is a quiet sigh, not a loud pop, and not a drop of wine lost.

Some red wines form a natural deposit as they age in bottle. When it is heavy, the wine needs decanting. Take the bottle out of the rack keeping it horizontal, ideally into a decanting basket, without stirring up the sediment. Gently remove the top of the capsule, clean the shoulder and neck, and ease out the cork. Then, holding the bottle in front of a light, pour slowly and steadily into the decanter, and stop as soon as you see the deposit reaching the neck.

Next, the glasses. There are hundreds of shapes, but the best all share one feature: the bowl narrows towards the rim, trapping and concentrating the aromas. Red wine glasses are usually a little larger than white wine glasses, and sparkling wine is served in a flute or a tulip-shaped glass. Glasses must be spotless: dirt or a trace of detergent can spoil a wine. Polish them before use to remove dust and fingermarks, with a clean, odour-free cloth.

Before pouring for guests, check the wine. Look at it: haziness could mean a fault. Make sure nothing is floating in it. Then smell it: a wine should not smell of wet cardboard or vinegar. It is much better to catch a problem in the bottle than in your guests' glasses.

Let's meet the three faults. Cork taint is caused by a chemical called TCA, mainly from contaminated corks, which is why we call such wines corked. It smells of damp cardboard, and the fruit seems muted and tired. A failed closure lets oxygen in, so the wine oxidises: it looks browner than it should, may smell of honey, caramel or coffee, and lacks freshness and fruit.

Be fair, though: some wines are made in an oxidative style on purpose, and very old wines can gain similar notes; it is only a fault in a wine that should be young and fruity. Finally, heat damage, from too much heat, sunlight or bright lights, leaves a wine stale and short of its expected fruit.

A memory tip for the faults: think of three Cs. Cardboard means cork taint. Caramel and a browner colour mean a closure that let air in. Cooked or flat fruit means the wine was kept too hot. And for opening sparkling wine, just remember: hand on the cork, turn the bottle.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, the temperature ladder runs from sweet wines and sparkling well chilled, through light whites and rosés chilled, full-bodied whites lightly chilled, light reds at thirteen to eighteen degrees, up to medium and full-bodied reds at fifteen to eighteen. Second, open sparkling wine with your hand always on the cork and turn the bottle, and decant wines with a heavy deposit, stopping when the sediment reaches the neck. Third, use clean glasses that narrow at the rim, check the wine before serving, and know the faults: cork taint smells of damp cardboard, oxidation from a failed closure gives a browner colour and caramel notes, and heat damage strips freshness and fruit.

In this lesson we sit down at the table. Food changes the way we perceive wine, and wine can change the way we perceive food. The aim of pairing is to use those effects so that the two together give more pleasure than either alone, and just as importantly, to avoid unpleasant clashes. We will look at the food components that matter most, sweetness, umami, acid and salt, then flavour intensity, fat and chilli heat, and finally how each of them affects sweetness, acidity, bitterness, fruitiness and alcohol in the wine.

First, a word about people. We do not all taste the same way. The same level of bitterness can hit one person hard and barely touch another. That is sensitivity. On top of that comes preference: some people enjoy a strong reaction, others dislike it. So a pairing one person calls perfect may seem ordinary, or even unpleasant, to someone else. A good pairing always considers the people at the table as well as the basic rules.

Why does food change wine? Because our taste buds adapt to whatever we have just eaten, and that shifts how we perceive the sugar, salt and acid in the next mouthful. Think of drinking orange juice just after brushing your teeth: suddenly it tastes harsh and sour. Some foods, like chocolate or thick creamy sauces, also coat the mouth and dull our sense of taste. And remember: food usually affects wine more than wine affects food, and the effect is more often negative than positive.

Here is the key idea of the whole lesson. Two food components make wine taste harder: sweetness and umami. A harder wine seems more drying and bitter, more acidic, less sweet and less fruity. Two other components make wine taste softer: salt and acid. A softer wine seems less drying and bitter, less acidic, sweeter and fruitier.

Let's start with sweetness. A sweet dish can make a dry wine seem less fruity and unpleasantly sour. So the rule is simple: with a sweet dish, choose a wine that is at least as sweet, ideally sweeter, than the food. A dry sparkling wine with a slice of wedding cake is a classic disappointment; a sweet wine will hold its own.

Umami is a savoury taste of its own, distinct from the others. It can be hard to spot because it usually comes with other tastes, such as salt, which soften its effect. Typical umami foods are cooked or dried mushrooms, air-dried meats, aged cheeses and miso. On its own, umami behaves like sweetness: it makes wine seem more bitter, more drying, more acidic and less fruity. Bitter, tannic reds are the most at risk.

Now the friendly components. Acid in food is generally good news. It can balance a wine with very high acidity, making the wine seem softer and fruitier. But if the wine itself is low in acidity, a sharp dish can make it taste flat and less fruity. So, with acidic food, pick a wine with at least as much acidity. Salt is the other friend. We salt food because it brings out flavour; even a plain boiled potato tastes of more with a pinch of salt. Salt does the same for wine: it makes it seem fruitier and fuller, and it softens the tannins of red wines.

Next, flavour intensity. Ideally the food and wine should be matched in intensity, so that one does not overwhelm the other. A delicate white with a heavily spiced stew will simply disappear; a powerful, oaky red can bury a delicate piece of white fish.

Fat and oil make a wine seem less acidic. That is why so many people love an acidic wine with fatty or fried food: the wine seems to cut through the richness and cleanse the palate, ready for the next bite. Like many of these effects, it is quite personal, but it is a widely enjoyed match.

Finally, chilli heat, a warming or burning sensation, and one where people differ enormously, both in sensitivity and in enjoyment. High alcohol makes the burn of chilli stronger, and the chilli also makes the alcohol in the wine more noticeable. So with spicy food, a wine with lower alcohol is the safer choice, unless your guest loves the fire.

A memory tip: think of two pairs of friends and foes. Sugar and umami are the troublemakers: they make wine hard, bitter and sour. Salt and acid are the peacemakers: they make wine soft and fruity. Then add three handy reminders: match the intensity, use acidity to cut through fat, and lower the alcohol when the chilli goes up.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, sweetness and umami in food make wine seem more bitter, drying and acidic and less sweet and fruity, so with sweet food choose a sweeter wine; umami comes from mushrooms, air-dried meats, aged cheeses and miso. Second, salt and acid make wine seem softer, fruitier and less acidic, with salt also softening tannin, while acidic food needs a wine with enough acidity. Third, match flavour intensity, enjoy acidic wines with fatty food, avoid high alcohol with chilli heat, and always remember that sensitivity and preference vary from person to person.

In this lesson we learn to taste like a professional. Tasting with a method means looking, smelling and tasting in the same order every time, and then drawing a conclusion about quality. At first it can feel repetitive, but with practice it becomes a habit you hardly notice. And good notes let you remember a wine, compare it with another, recommend it, or describe it to someone long after the bottle is empty.

First, set the scene. You need good light to judge the colour, a room free of strong smells, space for your glasses and notes, and somewhere to spit. Prepare yourself too: a clean palate, so no toothpaste or strongly flavoured food just before, and no perfume or aftershave, out of respect for the other tasters. The glass should be clean, clear and odour-free, with no traces of detergent. A good tasting glass has a rounded bowl for swirling and sides that slope inward to capture the aromas. Pour the same small amount each time, about fifty millilitres: enough to judge everything, little enough to swirl without spilling.

Step one is appearance. Almost all wines are clear; a hazy wine may be faulty, or simply unfiltered, and only the nose and palate will tell you which. Next, how deep is the colour? Tilt the glass and see how far the colour reaches from the core, the deepest point, out to the rim. A white with a wide watery rim is pale; one coloured almost to the edge is deep. For a red, you can also look down through the upright glass at the stem: if you see it easily, the wine is pale; if you cannot see it at all, it is deep.

Then the colour itself. Most whites are lemon; a touch of green tells you it is young and fresh, while gold, amber and finally brown suggest age, sweetness or oxidation. Most reds are ruby; purple hints mean youth, while garnet, then tawny, then brown show orange and brown tones creeping in with age. Rosés range from pure pink to pink with an orange tinge, and rarely to orange itself.

Step two is the nose. Swirl the wine to release its aromas, then take a short sniff. A quick sniff before swirling can also reveal delicate notes. Ask first: is the wine sound? Damp cardboard, unexpected honey, caramel or coffee, or a lack of freshness and fruit all point to a fault. Then judge intensity: if the aromas leap out as soon as your nose reaches the glass, they are strong; if you struggle to find them even after swirling, they are light; in between, medium.

Now describe the aromas, sorting them into three families. Primary aromas come from the grape and fermentation: fruit, flowers, green herbal notes, spice. Secondary aromas come from winemaking after fermentation: vanilla and smoke from oak, butter and cream from malolactic conversion, bread and biscuit from lees. Tertiary aromas come from ageing: with oxygen, as in a long time in barrel, you get coffee or caramel; protected from oxygen, as in a long time in bottle, you may find honey, petrol or mushroom. Ageing also makes fresh fruit taste dried. Work through these families like a checklist, but remember not every wine shows all three.

Step three is the palate, and you may need more than one sip. Sweetness: is there any sugar you can taste, from none at all to a little, to clearly present, to the main feature of the wine? Acidity: notice how much your mouth waters, and for how long. That watering is your most reliable guide, because sugar can mask acidity, and the burn of alcohol can feel like acidity.

Tannin, mostly in reds, comes from grape skins. It binds to your saliva, leaving the mouth dry and rough, sometimes with a bitter edge at the back. Alcohol adds weight and, when high, a warm or burning feeling, especially after you spit or swallow. Body is the overall feeling of weight in the mouth, built from all of these together: alcohol matters most, sugar adds body, high acidity makes a wine feel lighter, ripe tannin adds weight, and unripe tannin makes a wine feel thinner and harsher.

Then flavours. Usually they match the nose, though warmth in the mouth can bring out spice, and floral notes may fade, so note any changes. Finally the finish: how long do the pleasant sensations last after you spit or swallow? Count only the desirable ones. If the fruit vanishes and only acidity or bitterness lingers, the finish is short; if the flavours last as long as the structure, or longer, the finish is long.

Now the conclusion: how good is the wine? Most professionals agree on quality because they use four shared criteria. Balance: think of scales, with sugar balanced by acidity, and alcohol or acidity balanced by enough fruit. Length: a longer pleasant finish usually means higher quality, while a burning finish does not. Intensity: dilute flavours rarely make a good wine, though beyond a certain point more is not always better. Complexity: many aromas and flavours are often a plus, but some great wines shine through purity rather than complexity, icewines being a good example. The more of these four a wine satisfies, the higher its quality; one that fails all of them is poor, and a faulty wine sits apart.

A memory tip: think of a journey in four stops: look, smell, taste, decide. Look for clarity and colour. Smell for condition, intensity and the three aroma families. Taste for the structure, sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body, then flavour and finish. And decide using balance, length, intensity and complexity.

Before the quiz, remember three things. First, prepare well: good light, no strong smells, a clean palate and a clean, inward-curving glass with the same small sample each time. Second, follow the order: appearance, with clarity, depth and colour; nose, with condition, intensity and primary, secondary and tertiary aromas; palate, with sweetness, acidity judged by how much your mouth waters, tannin, alcohol, body, flavours and finish. Third, judge quality with four criteria, balance, length, intensity and complexity: the more a wine shows positively, the better it is.
